issues.title: Paying to be told no
issues.category_name: Visas, refusals and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: A visa fee buys consideration, not a visa, and it is not returned when the answer is no. Nigerians are refused at rates several times the global average, and the refused fees are a measurable national transfer to the refusing states.

details.aspect: The Schengen numbers
details.description: 111,201 Nigerians applied for Schengen visas in 2024 and 50,376 short-stay applications were refused - a 45.9% refusal rate, up from 40.5% in 2023 and the highest on record for Nigeria. At a non-refundable EUR 90 fee, that is over EUR 4.5 million, about NGN 7.1 billion, paid for refusals.
details.money_note: EUR 90 per application, non-refundable.
details.energy_note: Fifty thousand refusals, all paid for in advance.

details.aspect: The UK, over twenty-one years
details.description: The UK refused 1,344,595 Nigerian applications between 2005 and Q1 2026 - second only to India globally, and 15.2% of the 8.83 million refusals worldwide. Nigeria's cumulative refusal rate is 33.1%, more than double the UK's global average of 14.8%.
details.energy_note: One and a third million refusals, from one country.
details.source_name: UK Home Office entry clearance data

details.aspect: Where the UK refusals land
details.description: Visitor visas account for 1,127,088 of them - 83.8% of the total, at a 37.1% refusal rate. Study 130,712, work 41,410, family 12,217. The category most refused is the one used to attend a wedding, a graduation or a funeral.
details.energy_note: The visa you need to see your family is the one most refused.

details.aspect: The US rate, and the direction of travel
details.description: The US B1/B2 adjusted refusal rate for Nigeria was 57.00% in FY2025, up from 46.51% in FY2024 - against India at 22.04%. Ten points of deterioration in a single year.
details.energy_note: A coin flip, weighted against you, and getting worse.

details.aspect: The fees rise while the refusals do
details.description: UK visa fees went from GBP 100 to GBP 115 in July 2024 and GBP 127 in April 2025; the Schengen fee rose from EUR 80 to EUR 90 in June 2024. The cost of rejected UK visas rose 13.5% to GBP 50.7 million in 2024, with Nigerians paying an extra GBP 2 million.
details.energy_note: Charged more, each year, for the same refusal.

details.aspect: The true cost is a multiple of the fee
details.description: Biometrics appointments in another city, courier fees, bank statements, sponsor letters, notarised documents, travel insurance bought in advance, and flights held or booked. A refusal discards all of it.
details.money_note: Per attempt, everything beyond the fee itself.
details.energy_note: The fee is the cheapest part of being refused.

details.aspect: A refusal is a mark on the next application
details.description: Previous refusals must be declared and are weighed. The first no makes the second no more likely, which makes the third more likely still - a ratchet that no individual decision-maker has to intend.
details.energy_note: Refused once, and the file now says so forever.

details.aspect: So people stop applying, and that is invisible
details.description: The conference not attended, the job not interviewed for, the course not applied to. Nobody records a person who did not apply, so the true exclusion is larger than the refusal rate and will never appear in any dataset including this one.
details.energy_note: The applications never made are the real number.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - one wedding, four refusals
details.description: Her brother marries in Houston. Their mother, two sisters and an uncle apply together with the invitation, the hotel booking and the same sponsor letter. Three are refused. The family pays four fees and sends one person, who films it on a phone for the others.
details.money_note: Four non-refundable fees, one traveller.
details.energy_note: Four applications, one seat, and a video call.

details.aspect: The refusals that were never applications
details.description: The deepest layer of this issue is not the 45.9% refused. It is the people who read the rate, priced the fee against the odds, and did not apply - the scholarship not pursued, the conference declined, the sister's graduation watched online. That population is larger than the refused one and appears in no statistic anywhere.
details.energy_note: The largest category is the one nobody counts.

issues.title: Being cut to three months, single entry
issues.category_name: Visas, refusals and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: In July 2025 the United States reduced most non-immigrant visas for Nigerians to a single entry valid three months, replacing the five-year multiple-entry visas many held - and then suspended issuance entirely.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the reciprocity change, 8 July 2025
details.description: Effective immediately, most non-immigrant and non-diplomatic visas issued to Nigerian citizens became single-entry with three months' validity. The schedule was updated at the same time for Cameroon, Ethiopia and Ghana; at least 26 countries have seen validity reduced.
details.energy_note: Five years, reduced to twelve weeks, overnight.

details.aspect: What single entry actually means
details.description: Leaving the US at all - even briefly to a neighbouring country - means needing an entirely new visa stamp abroad before returning, regardless of whether the job or course is ongoing.
details.money_note: New application, fee and travel, per re-entry.
details.energy_note: One trip home, and you may not get back.

details.aspect: It lands hardest on students
details.description: Nigeria is America's seventh largest source of international students, sending over 20,000 in 2023/24. After three months a student must obtain a new visa each time they re-enter, with the fee each time.
details.energy_note: Twenty thousand students, each re-applying to go home for Christmas.

details.aspect: Then issuance stopped
details.description: New non-immigrant visa issuance was suspended from 1 January 2026 and immigrant visas from 21 January 2026. Reporting referenced a cable citing 36 countries considered for travel bans, and a court intervention over paused immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries including Nigeria.
details.energy_note: Not a harder queue. A closed window.

details.aspect: Nigeria disputes the reciprocity premise
details.description: Nigeria's presidential spokesperson said Nigeria continued to offer five-year multiple-entry visas to US nationals, refuting the claim that the change was reciprocal. The State Department framed its criteria around secure travel documents, overstay rates and information sharing.
details.energy_note: Called reciprocity, and reciprocated by nobody.

details.aspect: The planning horizon collapses to one trip
details.description: A multi-year visa lets a person accept a two-year posting, enrol in a three-year course, or plan a wedding abroad. A three-month single entry supports one journey and no commitments beyond it.
details.energy_note: You can plan exactly one trip at a time.

issues.title: Meeting every requirement and being refused anyway
issues.category_name: Visas, refusals and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The stated grounds are usually that the officer is not satisfied the applicant will leave. That is a prediction about the future, it cannot be disproved with documents, and it is not appealable in most categories.

details.aspect: The unfalsifiable ground
details.description: Strong ties, sufficient funds and a clean history do not answer a refusal based on the officer's assessment of intent. There is no document that proves what you will do in nine months.
details.energy_note: Refused for something that has not happened yet.

details.aspect: Nationality is doing work the letter does not mention
details.description: A Nigerian applicant with the same salary, assets and travel history as an applicant of another nationality faces a materially different probability. The refusal letter never says so and the aggregate statistics do.
details.energy_note: Same file, different passport, different answer.

details.aspect: The appeal route mostly does not exist
details.description: Visitor refusals generally carry no right of appeal, only reapplication - which means paying the fee again to be assessed by the same standard, with a refusal now on record.
details.energy_note: The remedy is to pay again.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the conference in Amsterdam
details.description: Her abstract is accepted in February for a June conference. The appointment is in April, the refusal arrives in May citing insufficient evidence of intent to return, and the EUR 90 is gone. Her co-author presents both halves of the paper and is asked a question she could have answered.
details.energy_note: Published, funded, and absent.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the wedding in Milan
details.description: Her sister is marrying in June. She applies in March with the invitation, the hotel, the return flight and six months of payslips. The refusal cites insufficient evidence of socio-economic ties. She watches it on a video call from her office in Ikoyi with the sound low.
details.energy_note: Refused for the wedding, and at work that day.

issues.title: The agent who filled in your form
issues.category_name: Visas, refusals and the money spent on being told no
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Where the process is opaque and the stakes are high, an industry of agents appears. Some are useful, many are extractive, and a few enter information the applicant has never seen - which the applicant is then held responsible for.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the official warning about agents
details.description: Nigeria's diaspora commission, explaining a case of travellers refused entry in South Africa, said visa agents complete application sections without travellers' full knowledge, leaving applicants unable to verify their own information when questioned at the port of entry.
details.energy_note: Interrogated about answers you never gave.

details.aspect: The applicant carries the consequence, not the agent
details.description: A discrepancy between what the form says and what the traveller says is treated as deception by the traveller. The agent is not present, not named and not liable.
details.energy_note: Accused of lying about a sentence someone else typed.

details.aspect: And a misrepresentation finding is long-lived
details.description: A finding of deception can carry a multi-year bar in several jurisdictions - a penalty far exceeding the refusal itself, arising from an error the applicant may not have known existed.
details.energy_note: A decade barred, over someone else's typing.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the agent's bank statement
details.description: The agent said he would 'strengthen' her application. At the interview the officer asks about a NGN 14 million balance she has never had. She says she does not recognise it. The refusal is recorded as misrepresentation and carries a ten-year bar.
details.energy_note: A decade barred, for a number she never typed.

issues.title: A passport that ranks 90th and shrinks
issues.category_name: The passport, the booklet racket and proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The Nigerian passport reaches 44 destinations without a prior visa. The number has been falling, and the long-run trend is downward against peers.

details.aspect: Where it sits
details.description: 90th in the July 2026 Henley Passport Index, down one place, with 44 destinations reachable visa-free or visa-on-arrival. Other indices differ by method: Passport Index lists 25 visa-free with a power rank of 91, and VisaGuide places Nigeria 189th of 199 with 28.
details.energy_note: Forty-four doors, out of roughly two hundred.

details.aspect: The long trend is the real story
details.description: Nigeria has fallen roughly 26 places in twenty years, from 62nd in 2006. One tracker records a drop from 46 destinations in January 2025 to 44 in May 2026 - the number shrinking rather than growing.
details.energy_note: Twenty-six places down in twenty years.

details.aspect: Regional peers do better, which removes the easy explanation
details.description: Ghana and Senegal rank higher through broader bilateral arrangements in South America and Asia. The constraint is diplomatic and reputational, not geographic or continental.
details.energy_note: Not an Africa problem. A Nigeria problem.

details.aspect: Every closed door is an application
details.description: Each destination not on the list means a fee, an appointment, documents, a wait and a refusal risk - so the passport's weakness converts directly into the costs recorded in VIS-001.
details.energy_note: The ranking is a bill, paid per trip.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the destinations that are not destinations
details.description: The forty-four include several she will never go to and excludes every country she has professional reason to visit. The headline number is not a measure of where she can go; it is a measure of where nobody objects to her going.
details.energy_note: Forty-four places, and none of them the conference.

issues.title: The booklet that is not there
issues.category_name: The passport, the booklet racket and proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Getting the passport at all is a hurdle before it is used. Booklets run short, the portal shows 'processing' for months, and the people who pay privately are served first.

details.aspect: Nigeria does not print its own booklets
details.description: Despite owning a minting and printing company, Nigeria does not produce passport booklets. A 2021 shortage was tied to government debts to a foreign technical partner that refused to supply; in 2024 booklets were scarce nationwide for over a month ahead of an approved price increase.
details.energy_note: The document proving you are Nigerian is printed abroad, on credit.

details.aspect: The price tripled, and the racket did not stop
details.description: The standard booklet fee rose from NGN 35,000 to NGN 100,000 in August 2025, defended as an anti-corruption measure. Immigration officers themselves said the higher cost would not end racketeering, citing processing fees charged through system loopholes and the practical need for middlemen outside Lagos and Abuja.
details.money_note: NGN 35,000 to NGN 100,000, official fee alone.
details.energy_note: Tripled the price, kept the bribe.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - two neighbours, one payment
details.description: An applicant who applied in August 2025 was still seeing 'processing' on the portal in January 2026, while a neighbour who applied the same day received his passport within weeks after paying an officer.
details.money_note: The informal payment that moves the file.
details.energy_note: Same day, same office, five months apart.

details.aspect: The digital portal did not remove the officer
details.description: A 2022 investigation found the 2019 e-passport portal failed to stem bribe demands, with officials hoarding booklets and inventing fees for applicants who would not pay.
details.energy_note: Digitised, and still transacted in cash.

details.aspect: Renewal abroad is worse
details.description: Nigerians abroad report extortion and delays at consulates, where the queue is longer, the alternatives are none, and an expired passport puts the holder's residence status at risk in the host country.
details.energy_note: Your visa depends on a consulate that is not answering.

details.aspect: A late passport cascades into everything else
details.description: A job offer with a start date, a course with an enrolment deadline, a visa appointment already booked, a residence permit expiring. The booklet is upstream of all of them.
details.energy_note: One missing booklet, four missed deadlines.

issues.title: Proving you are who you say, repeatedly
issues.category_name: The passport, the booklet racket and proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Identity in Nigeria is assembled from several partial systems - NIN, BVN, voter card, driver's licence, certificate of origin - none of which is sufficient alone, and each of which requires the others.

details.aspect: Several registries, no single truth
details.description: The bank wants a BVN, the phone company a NIN, the state a certificate of indigeneship, the employer a birth certificate. Each enrolment needs documents the others issue.
details.energy_note: A circle of systems, each demanding the others.

details.aspect: Enrolment is a day, or several
details.description: Queues at enrolment centres, systems offline, biometrics failing, forms reprinted. The cost is not the fee; it is the working days.
details.energy_note: Three days off work to obtain a number.

details.aspect: Women's records break at marriage
details.description: A name change on marriage must be propagated across every registry separately, and any registry not updated produces a mismatch that is treated as the woman's error.
details.energy_note: Married, and now inconsistent across six databases.

details.aspect: Certificate of indigeneship follows the husband, not the woman
details.description: Indigeneship is tied to origin, and a married woman is frequently treated as an indigene of neither her birth state nor her husband's - one of the specific gaps the 2022 gender bills tried to close and failed.
details.energy_note: From nowhere, officially, once you marry.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the enrolment centre at 6am
details.description: She arrives at six to be forty-first in the queue. The system is down until eleven. At two the operator says the fingerprint scanner will not read her right thumb - she has traded dried fish for nine years - and she should come back with a letter.
details.energy_note: Biometrics that cannot read a working hand.

issues.title: Documents that are assumed to be forged
issues.category_name: The passport, the booklet racket and proving who you are
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Nigerian civil and academic documents attract verification demands that documents from other countries do not, at the applicant's cost and on the applicant's time.

details.aspect: Verification is routine rather than exceptional
details.description: Degrees, transcripts, birth and marriage certificates and police clearances are sent for third-party verification as standard - a step applied selectively by country of issue.
details.energy_note: Genuine, and checked anyway, because of where it is from.

details.aspect: The verifying body may not answer
details.description: Where the issuing institution is slow, unreachable or was affected by a strike, an unanswered verification is treated as a failed one and the application closes.
details.energy_note: Your degree is real and unconfirmable.

details.aspect: The suspicion is not baseless and is applied collectively
details.description: Document fraud exists, and it is a small fraction of applicants. The response is applied to the nationality rather than to the indicators, which is the mechanism this whole dataset keeps recording.
details.energy_note: A minority's fraud, charged to everyone's paperwork.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the police clearance that arrives after the offer
details.description: The employer needs a certificate of good conduct. It takes eleven weeks. The start date was in six. The role is filled by someone whose clearance took four days because they were applying from a different country.
details.energy_note: Lost the job to a faster police force.

issues.title: The second room
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The brief asks about unusually high rates of random checks. The honest position: the mechanics are documented, the referral criteria are published in outline, and no government publishes a per-nationality secondary-inspection rate - so the disparity is attested by consistent reporting rather than by a statistic.

details.aspect: How the referral works
details.description: Every traveller goes through primary inspection. Some are sent to secondary. One legal account puts roughly 5% of arrivals as referred at random, with many more referred for cause - a database hit, a watchlist match, a travel-pattern anomaly, a social media flag, a tip from another agency, or an unresolved prior immigration record.
details.energy_note: Five per cent at random, and then the rest for reasons.

details.aspect: What the visa actually entitles you to
details.description: A visa permits travel to a port of entry and a request for admission. It does not guarantee entry; an officer at the port decides admissibility after arrival, regardless of the years spent obtaining the visa.
details.energy_note: Every approval you obtained, overridable at the desk.

details.aspect: What happens in the room
details.description: Waiting hours, missing connections, being asked the same question repeatedly while officers review prior entries, visa applications, arrests and petitions. Inspections run from 30 minutes to many hours.
details.money_note: Missed connections and rebooked flights, per occurrence.
details.energy_note: Four hours, and the connecting flight is gone.

details.aspect: Your phone is searchable without a warrant
details.description: At a port of entry, Fourth and Fifth Amendment protections are sharply reduced. CBP can search phones without a warrant under the border search exception, and can send visa holders home on the next flight.
details.energy_note: Your messages, read, lawfully, while you wait.

details.aspect: HONEST GAP - there is no published per-nationality rate
details.description: No systematic data or civil-rights finding was located showing Nigerian travellers are disproportionately referred to secondary. The publicly available CBP material on Nigerians is agency-published enforcement cases, which is not evidence of a pattern. The disparity is widely reported by travellers and is not, at present, a published statistic.
details.energy_note: Everybody experiences the rate. Nobody publishes it.
details.notes: Handled the same way as AIR-001 in assets/text/palestine. Stating the gap is more useful than inventing a number.

details.aspect: So the adaptation is defensive and permanent
details.description: Arrive four hours early. Never book a tight connection. Carry the invitation letter, the bank statements, the return ticket and the hotel booking in print. Assume the phone will be read. This is unpaid preparation performed before every single journey.
details.money_note: Annual cost of defensive travel planning.
details.energy_note: Packing for an interrogation, every time.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the four hours at Atlanta
details.description: She is referred at 06:40. Her connection to Raleigh is at 09:15. At 09:50 an officer returns her passport, says nothing further, and points at the exit. The airline rebooks her for 18:20 and charges the change fee, because the delay was not the airline's.
details.energy_note: Cleared, with no explanation, and billed for the delay.

details.aspect: The preparation becomes a personality
details.description: Print everything. Arrive absurdly early. Never book a connection under three hours. Assume the phone will be read, so curate it beforehand. After a decade this is no longer a set of precautions; it is simply how the person travels, and they no longer notice they are doing it.
details.energy_note: Defensive travel, absorbed into the character.

issues.title: Deportation, and the third country
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Removal is not only to Nigeria. Third-country arrangements mean a Nigerian removed from one state may be delivered to another entirely.

details.aspect: The docket
details.description: Roughly 3,690 Nigerians in the United States face deportation, drawn from ICE data showing 1,445,549 non-citizens on the non-detained docket with final removal orders as of 24 November 2024.
details.energy_note: Three thousand six hundred and ninety names on a list.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - removed to Ghana, then bussed
details.description: In September 2025 Ghana's president said a group of 14 deportees including Nigerians and one Gambian had arrived in Ghana, with the government facilitating the Nigerians' onward return home by bus - part of an arrangement under which Ghana accepts third-country nationals removed from the US, limited to West African nationals.
details.energy_note: Deported to a country you are not from, then put on a coach.

details.aspect: The removal severs everything at once
details.description: Employment, tenancy, bank accounts, a course mid-way, and frequently children who remain. There is no wind-down period and no mechanism to return for one.
details.energy_note: A life ended by an itinerary.

details.aspect: Re-entry bars follow
details.description: Removal typically carries a multi-year or permanent bar on return, so a family split by a deportation is split for the length of the bar rather than the length of the flight.
details.energy_note: Ten years, before you may even apply again.

issues.title: Being the nationality the airline worries about
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Carriers bear fines for bringing inadmissible passengers, so they screen before departure - which moves part of the border to the check-in desk in Lagos.

details.aspect: Carrier liability pushes checks upstream
details.description: Airlines face penalties for carrying passengers refused entry, so ground staff verify visas, onward tickets and sometimes funds - applying a standard that varies by route and by passport.
details.energy_note: Questioned at check-in, before any border.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - refused departure from their own country
details.description: In 2020 Nigeria's Immigration Service refused departure to 58 London-bound Nigerian doctors at Lagos airport; the chartered flight was meant to carry 42 for training and 58 presented, of whom only two held UK visas.
details.energy_note: Stopped from leaving, by your own immigration service.

details.aspect: Denied boarding is worse than denied entry
details.description: A refusal at the gate means the ticket is used, the visa clock runs, and the traveller is in their own country with no incident to appeal and no record anyone will produce.
details.energy_note: Refused by an airline, with nothing to appeal.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the funds question at check-in
details.description: Ground staff ask how much money she is carrying and where she is staying. The passenger behind her, going to the same city, is asked nothing. Both have valid visas. The airline is applying its own risk assessment and is entitled to.
details.energy_note: Asked at the desk what the border would have asked.

issues.title: The exit interview at your own departure
issues.category_name: Airports abroad, screening and the second room
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Leaving Nigeria involves its own layers - immigration, security, sometimes a trafficking screening that is necessary in design and intrusive in execution, and which falls hardest on young women travelling alone.

details.aspect: Anti-trafficking screening at departure
details.description: Because of the documented trafficking routes in TRF-001, young women travelling alone are questioned about their purpose, sponsor, destination and relationship to whoever paid. The screening exists for good reason and is experienced as an accusation.
details.energy_note: Protected, in a way that feels exactly like suspicion.

details.aspect: The genuine traveller has no way to distinguish herself
details.description: A student with a scholarship and a trafficked woman with a coached story present similarly at a desk. The officer has minutes. The error runs in both directions and both errors are serious.
details.energy_note: An impossible judgement, made in ninety seconds.

details.aspect: Which creates the opening for extortion
details.description: A discretionary hold that can be released is a hold that can be sold. Informal payments at departure are widely reported and rarely recorded.
details.energy_note: A fee to be allowed onto a flight you paid for.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the master's student
details.description: Twenty-four, funded place in Leeds, September start. At the desk she is asked who is paying, why a woman her age is travelling alone, and whether her family approve. She has the letter, the bank statement and the visa. She answers for forty minutes and makes the flight by eleven.
details.energy_note: Forty minutes of proving she is not being sold.

issues.title: Refused entry with valid documents
issues.category_name: Borders, entry refusals and being turned around
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: A visa is permission to ask. Documented cases show Nigerians with valid visas, return tickets, accommodation and funds refused entry, detained for days, and removed - sometimes to a third country.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - eighty hours at Sal Airport, then Senegal
details.description: The Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa filed a case before the ECOWAS Court of Justice against Cabo Verde on behalf of five Nigerian travellers, alleging that despite valid travel documents, return tickets, accommodation and sufficient funds they were singled out at Sal Airport, detained over 80 hours and deported to Senegal in April 2025.
details.energy_note: Everything in order, and eighty hours in a room.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - watchlisted for a social media post
details.description: Three Nigerians denied entry at OR Tambo in April 2026 said they were unlawfully detained despite valid visas, and that a phone was seized. Nigeria's diaspora commission said one had been flagged for previously making insulting remarks about the South African government online, placing him on a watchlist.
details.energy_note: Refused entry over an old post about the government.

details.aspect: ECOWAS free movement is a right with a desk in front of it
details.description: Nigerians hold a regional free-movement entitlement that is nonetheless administered by individual officers at individual airports, which is why a case had to be filed to establish it.
details.energy_note: A right that required a court to notice.

details.aspect: The cost of a refusal at the far end
details.description: Return flight, the nights held, the purpose of the trip lost, and in several cases the phone or documents retained. None of it is compensated.
details.energy_note: Paid for the trip, then paid to come back.

issues.title: Refused for travelling without a man
issues.category_name: Borders, entry refusals and being turned around
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: The clearest single intersection in this dataset: a state refused entry to hundreds of Nigerian women, not for anything about them, but because they arrived without a husband or male relative.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Jeddah, September 2012
details.description: Saudi immigration officials refused entry to hundreds of Nigerian women pilgrims for not travelling with a husband or male relative. Around 509 would-be pilgrims were affected, some held at the airport for as long as five days. Nigeria suspended pilgrimage flights to Saudi Arabia in response.
details.money_note: Pilgrimage cost, largely unrecoverable.
details.energy_note: Five hundred and nine women, refused for arriving alone.

details.aspect: Two rule systems, one woman
details.description: She satisfied every Nigerian requirement to depart and every documentary requirement to arrive. The refusal rested on a condition about her companions, which no document could satisfy.
details.energy_note: Compliant with both countries, and refused by one.

details.aspect: The saving was a lifetime's
details.description: Hajj is frequently the single largest discretionary expenditure of a person's life, saved for over years. The refusal did not refund it.
details.energy_note: A lifetime's saving, spent on five days in an airport.

details.aspect: The pattern recurs in the labour routes
details.description: The same principle - that a woman's movement is conditioned on a man's presence or permission - reappears in the Gulf employment contracts in TRF-002, where the permission is the employer's.
details.energy_note: Different country, same clause.

details.aspect: And it is invisible in the aggregate statistics
details.description: Refusals like this are recorded, if at all, as entry refusals. Nothing in the data says the ground was the absence of a male relative, so the phenomenon does not appear in any dataset of gendered barriers.
details.energy_note: Counted as a refusal. Not counted as a gendered one.

issues.title: Coming home, and the desk at that end too
issues.category_name: Borders, entry refusals and being turned around
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Return is not frictionless either. Arrival in Nigeria involves its own informal costs, and for deportees and returnees a reception that is administrative rather than supportive.

details.aspect: Informal payments on arrival
details.description: Requests at immigration, customs and baggage are widely reported by returning Nigerians. Small individually, they are a levy on every homecoming.
details.energy_note: Paying a little, to enter your own country.

details.aspect: Deportees arrive to nothing
details.description: Groups returned involuntarily have historically arrived with no money, no documents beyond a travel certificate, and no reintegration provision - 'dazed and confused', as one contemporaneous report of 48 returnees put it.
details.energy_note: Landed, released into the car park, and that is the programme.

details.aspect: Returning is socially expensive as well
details.description: A return without visible success is read as failure by an extended family that may have funded the journey, which is why some people stay abroad in worse conditions than they would accept at home.
details.energy_note: Staying away because coming back would have to be explained.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the returning graduate
details.description: Seven years abroad, a master's, and a suitcase. Immigration is unremarkable. It is the aunties at the arrivals gate, counting what he brought and not finding the car, who deliver the actual assessment.
details.energy_note: Cleared by immigration, assessed at the barrier.

issues.title: Claiming asylum from a country nobody calls a war
issues.category_name: Status abroad: asylum, deportation and the years in between
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Nigeria is not at war in the way decision-makers picture, so a Nigerian claim starts from a presumption of safety and must dismantle it - which is a different and harder task than arriving from a recognised conflict.

details.aspect: The Canadian acceptance gap
details.description: Over a ten-year window 39% of Nigerian refugee claimants were approved against an overall acceptance rate of 58%. CBC's analysis put Nigerian acceptance at 46% between 2018 and September 2024, against an overall recognition rate that rose to 82% in the first nine months of 2024.
details.energy_note: Half the odds of the average claimant, on the same evidence standard.

details.aspect: And the volume of refusals
details.description: Between 2013 and 2024 Canada's Refugee Protection Division denied 13,171 Nigerian applications and accepted 10,580, putting Nigeria consistently among the top five countries for asylum denials, peaking at 3,951 refusals in 2019.
details.energy_note: Thirteen thousand refusals from one country.

details.aspect: Everything goes to a hearing
details.description: An immigration lawyer describes cases from countries with historically lower acceptance rates, like Nigeria, as always sent to hearings - where the claimant must prove the police cannot protect her and that she could not be safe anywhere else in the country.
details.energy_note: No paper decision. Always the room, always the cross-examination.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 'she could have moved to a large city'
details.description: The Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers challenged the IRB's decision to set as a legal precedent its denial of a Nigerian woman's claim based on female genital mutilation, where it was found she could have relocated to one of Nigeria's large cities. Internal flight alternative is the mechanism by which a real danger becomes a survivable one on paper.
details.energy_note: The cutting was real. The finding was that she should have moved.

details.aspect: The UK route narrows at the certification stage
details.description: The UK initial grant rate across all nationalities fell from a record 76% in 2022 to 47% by 2024 and 39% currently. Claims certified as clearly unfounded under section 94 carry no in-country appeal, and since 28 June 2022 section 94(3A) means a certified claim carries no appeal at all.
details.energy_note: Refused, certified, and no appeal exists.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the returns agreement, by the numbers
details.description: A UK-Nigeria returns agreement targeted 961 Nigerian asylum seekers with no appeal rights remaining and 1,110 foreign national offenders in prisons. In the year ending September 2025 Nigerians ranked among the top five nationalities claiming asylum after entering the UK on a valid visa, and the Home Office said this led it to tighten visa and asylum grants to Nigerians.
details.energy_note: A quota with a nationality on it.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the credibility finding
details.description: She cannot name the date her uncle came to the house, because she was fourteen and there was no calendar on the wall. The determination notes the inconsistency between her screening interview and her substantive interview and finds her account not credible. Everything she said was true.
details.energy_note: Disbelieved over a date she was never told.

details.aspect: The waiting is the punishment even when you win
details.description: Years without the right to work, on subsistence support, in accommodation chosen for you, with the case reopening at intervals. A grant at the end does not return the years.
details.money_note: Foregone earnings across the wait.
details.energy_note: Four years of not being allowed to work.

issues.title: Germany: refused, and deported to Italy
issues.category_name: Status abroad: asylum, deportation and the years in between
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The Dublin system means a Nigerian claim in Germany is frequently not decided on its merits at all, but declared inadmissible and routed to the first EU country of entry - and if that transfer fails, the clock restarts.

details.aspect: The community and the caseload
details.description: Around 72,000 people of Nigerian origin lived in Germany as of November 2019, the largest sub-Saharan African community in the country. BAMF expanded the number of offices handling Nigerian asylum claims because Nigeria became one of the ten largest countries of origin worldwide.
details.energy_note: Large enough community to need its own processing capacity.

details.aspect: The formal-decision share, and what observers conclude from it
details.description: Reporting notes the proportion of purely formal decisions on Nigerian applications is very high compared with other countries of origin, with the conclusion drawn that Black refugees are not especially welcome. A formal decision is one that never reaches the question of whether the person is in danger.
details.energy_note: Decided without anyone asking what happened to you.

details.aspect: The Dublin loop
details.description: BAMF frequently declares claims inadmissible under Dublin and orders removal to Italy. If the transfer is not effected within six months, Germany becomes responsible again and the procedure begins afresh - so the applicant waits, is told to leave, is not moved, and starts over.
details.energy_note: Six months of being about to be deported, then back to the start.

details.aspect: Most deportations of Nigerians are not to Nigeria
details.description: Many people with Nigerian nationality are deported each year, but predominantly to Italy rather than to Nigeria. The removal is intra-European and the person's actual country never enters the transaction.
details.energy_note: Deported, and not to the country you are from.

details.aspect: Missing travel documents suspend removals, which helps nobody
details.description: The commonest reason deportations are suspended is a lack of travel documents, with the Nigerian embassy slow to issue them. The result is not safety but limbo: not removable, not regularised, not permitted to work.
details.energy_note: Unremovable and unsettled, at the same time.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - refused for being able to hide
details.description: A Nigerian man in his early thirties claimed asylum in Germany on grounds of persecution for his homosexuality. BAMF argued it was disputed how strongly the relevant legislation is enforced, and refused; he litigated. Rejecting queer claimants on the basis that they could conceal themselves at home has been repeatedly criticised as unlawful.
details.energy_note: Refused because the law against you is only sometimes enforced.

issues.title: The years with no status and no exit
issues.category_name: Status abroad: asylum, deportation and the years in between
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Between refusal and removal there is a condition with no name: not lawful, not removable, not permitted to work, and not permitted to leave and return.

details.aspect: No right to work is the whole of it
details.description: Without work authorisation there is no lawful income, which means informal work at whatever rate is offered, with no recourse for non-payment because complaining requires identifying yourself.
details.energy_note: Working, and unable to say so, or to be paid properly.

details.aspect: Healthcare narrows to emergencies
details.description: Chronic conditions go unmanaged because registration requires status. The diabetes, the fibroids, the hypertension all progress until they qualify as an emergency, which is the most expensive possible point of treatment.
details.energy_note: Waiting until it is an emergency, because that is the only door.

details.aspect: Reporting conditions structure the week
details.description: Signing at a police station or reporting centre at intervals, with the possibility of detention at each one, means no job with fixed hours and no journey longer than the gap between reports.
details.time_note: Days per year consumed by reporting.
details.energy_note: A life sized to fit between two signings.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - eleven years
details.description: She arrived at twenty-six. She is thirty-seven. She has been refused twice, appealed once, made fresh submissions twice, and been detained for nine days in 2021. She has an English accent now. She has never had a National Insurance number.
details.energy_note: A decade spent being about to be deported.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the reporting centre
details.description: Every second Tuesday, 9am, forty minutes on two buses. She has done it sixty-one times. She has never been detained at one and she has never once walked in without considering that she might be.
details.energy_note: Sixty-one Tuesdays of walking in wondering.

issues.title: Regularising, and the fee that is the barrier
issues.category_name: Status abroad: asylum, deportation and the years in between
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Where a route to status exists, it is priced - and the price is set at a level that functions as the actual eligibility criterion.

details.aspect: Fees per person, per application, per cycle
details.description: Applications for leave to remain are charged per applicant, so a family of four pays four times, on a route that may require several grants before settlement. A health surcharge is levied on top, in advance, for the full period.
details.money_note: Per cycle, per family, plus surcharge in advance.
details.energy_note: Charged per head, per cycle, for a decade.

details.aspect: Missing a renewal converts lawful to unlawful overnight
details.description: A late application, often caused by not having the fee on the date, ends continuous residence and can reset a ten-year route to zero.
details.energy_note: Nine years of compliance, voided by one late payment.

details.aspect: Legal help is the difference and is not funded
details.description: The difference between a granted and refused application is frequently the quality of the submission. Representation costs money that the fees have already taken.
details.energy_note: Needing a lawyer you spent the lawyer's fee on the form.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the family that split by arithmetic
details.description: Four applications, and enough money for three. They apply for the children and the mother. The father's leave lapses. He is now the one who cannot work, in the house he is paying for.
details.energy_note: A family made illegal by a budget.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the health surcharge
details.description: The application is GBP 1,048 each plus the surcharge for three years, payable at submission, for four people. She works it out twice because the first total seemed wrong. It was not wrong.
details.energy_note: Four people, three years, paid in advance, in one transaction.

issues.title: Being read as a fraud before you speak
issues.category_name: The 419 inheritance: being read as a fraud before you speak
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: No other nationality in this set of datasets carries a scam as its global shorthand. 'Nigerian prince' is a punchline in languages that have no other Nigerian referent, and it arrives in the room before the person does.

details.aspect: The name comes from a section of the criminal code
details.description: '419' is Section 419 of the Nigerian Criminal Code, which deals with obtaining by false pretences. By 1995 the association was strong enough that Nigeria amended its criminal code specifically to address the fraud, and the government has estimated that advance-fee scams damaged Nigeria's international reputation more than any other factor.
details.energy_note: A national reputation, named after a paragraph number.

details.aspect: The format is older than Nigeria's involvement in it
details.description: The structure predates the country entirely: the 18th-century 'Spanish Prisoner' con promised a reward to anyone paying for a trapped relative's release. Nigeria's name attached to it by an accident of timing - cheap fax and email arriving alongside an economic collapse.
details.energy_note: An eighteenth-century European con, filed under your country.

details.aspect: THE IRONY THAT MATTERS - the scammers do not present as Nigerian
details.description: In a study of 50 convicted romance scammers, 46% posed as white American males, 12% as military personnel and 10% as white European males. Posing as white is the standard tactic. So the men actually running the fraud are invisible as Nigerians, while ordinary Nigerians using their real names and faces absorb the entire suspicion.
details.energy_note: The scammer is pretending to be American. You are the one who looks Nigerian.
details.notes: This single row is the logical centre of the REP category.

details.aspect: The scale of the losses that fuel the reputation
details.description: FTC data put total US romance scam losses at $1.14 billion in 2023 with more than 64,000 victims. The harm is real, which is precisely why the collective attribution is so hard to argue against.
details.energy_note: The damage is real. The billing of it to 220 million people is not.

details.aspect: The socioeconomic engine, stated without excusing it
details.description: Among convicted offenders studied, 81.7% were under 26 and 74% were university students, against youth unemployment estimated at 53.4% for 15-to-34-year-olds and average monthly income comparable to 1980 levels.
details.energy_note: Mostly students, mostly under twenty-six, mostly with nothing else.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the introduction
details.description: She says where she is from at a work social. There is a half-second pause, and then someone makes the prince joke, and everyone laughs including her, because the alternative is to be the person who could not take it. She has done this perhaps two hundred times.
details.energy_note: Laughing at it, again, because not laughing costs more.

details.aspect: The professional cost compounds silently
details.description: Slower trust, more verification, fewer introductions, more scrutiny of the same work. None of it appears in a performance review and all of it accumulates across a career.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings effect of a reputational headwind.
details.energy_note: A career run at a slightly worse exchange rate.

issues.title: Yahoo boys, and the men who are not them
issues.category_name: The 419 inheritance: being read as a fraud before you speak
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The domestic term for internet fraudsters has become an international descriptor for young Nigerian men generally, including the overwhelming majority who are not involved.

details.aspect: Where the word came from
details.description: 'Yahoo boys' are named for the email service that became popular in Nigeria in the 2000s, and are described as descendants of the 419 scammers. Nigeria and Ghana are characterised as the continent's internet-fraud hubs, alongside Ghana's 'Sakawa boys'.
details.energy_note: A local slang term, now an international category.

details.aspect: Domestic opinion is split, which complicates the defence
details.description: Inside Nigeria some see them as criminals who marred the country's reputation; others treat them as folk heroes taking money from white foreigners as reparation. Interviews with offenders in Ghana found they framed their actions as legitimate retribution for colonial injustice.
details.energy_note: Not a united front to point at, which the outside reads as consent.

details.aspect: A young man's visible success becomes evidence against him
details.description: A car, a laptop, foreign currency, unexplained travel - ordinary markers of a good job that, for a young Nigerian man, function as suspicion in both directions: from foreign institutions and from Nigerian police.
details.energy_note: Doing well is itself the accusation.

details.aspect: HONEST GAP - the platform-blocking claim is not documented
details.description: No sourced evidence was located that Nigerian men are algorithmically profiled or blocked on dating platforms specifically. The reputational mechanism is well documented; that particular application of it is reported anecdotally and is recorded here as unverified.
details.energy_note: Widely said, not yet demonstrated.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the video call that was the interview
details.description: The contract was agreed over email. On the call the client sees his face and hears Lagos behind him, and asks, pleasantly, whether he can do a short unpaid trial first. There was no trial in the original scope.
details.energy_note: The terms changed when they saw him.

issues.title: Guilty until verified, at every institution
issues.category_name: The 419 inheritance: being read as a fraud before you speak
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: The reputational default converts into procedure: more documents, more checks, longer holds, and a higher bar for the same transaction.

details.aspect: The verification tax
details.description: Additional identity documents, notarisation, source-of-funds evidence and manual review on transactions that would clear automatically for another nationality.
details.energy_note: Everything takes three extra steps, forever.

details.aspect: Nobody ever states it, so it cannot be challenged
details.description: The letter cites policy. The call-centre agent cites the system. There is no decision-maker to appeal to and no finding to contest.
details.energy_note: A rule with no author and no appeal.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the deposit
details.description: Her first freelance payment from a UK client is held for review. On day nine she is asked for the contract, the client's company registration, and an explanation of the relationship. She supplies all three. On day nineteen it clears. Her rent was due on day five.
details.energy_note: Paid on time, and late anyway.

details.aspect: The rational adaptation is to hide the nationality
details.description: Using a foreign address, a relative's account, a non-Nigerian company, or simply not mentioning Lagos. Each works, each costs money or honesty, and each confirms to the person that the identity is the problem.
details.energy_note: Succeeding by not being from where you are from.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the invoice that needed a phone call
details.description: Her UK client's finance department will not release a payment to a Nigerian account without verbal confirmation from the client, who is on leave. The invoice is for GBP 900 and the verification process has now cost more of her time than the work did.
details.energy_note: More hours verifying the payment than earning it.

issues.title: What it does to a person to be a punchline
issues.category_name: The 419 inheritance: being read as a fraud before you speak
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Distinct from the economic cost: the internal effect of belonging to a nationality that is a globally recognised joke about dishonesty.

details.aspect: Pre-emptive over-documentation
details.description: Nigerians describe volunteering evidence nobody asked for - references, certificates, receipts - to forestall a doubt that has not yet been expressed. It is exhausting and it is rational.
details.energy_note: Proving yourself before anyone has doubted you.

details.aspect: Anger at the actual fraudsters, which has nowhere to go
details.description: The resentment among ordinary Nigerians towards the people who built the reputation is intense, and expressing it abroad reads as confirming the stereotype rather than distancing from it.
details.energy_note: Furious at them, and unable to say so without sounding like them.

details.aspect: Children inherit it without the context
details.description: Second-generation children are asked about the prince joke in a playground in a country their parents chose, with no framework for it and no memory of Nigeria at all.
details.energy_note: A nine-year-old in Croydon, explaining 419.

details.aspect: It suppresses the very thing that would change it
details.description: Visibility - starting the company, taking the platform, publishing under your own name - is what would eventually replace the stereotype, and it is exactly what the stereotype makes costly.
details.energy_note: The cure is the thing it makes expensive.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the homework question
details.description: His daughter is nine, born in Manchester, and asks at dinner what a Nigerian prince is, because a boy at school said it. He has about four seconds to decide how much of the last thirty years to explain to a nine-year-old.
details.energy_note: Four seconds to decide how much to tell her.

issues.title: Twenty years without PayPal
issues.category_name: Banking, cards and payment exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: From 2004 to 2026 Nigerians could not receive money through the world's default consumer payment platform. The exclusion was explicit, national, and outlasted the conditions given for it.

details.aspect: The timeline
details.description: In 2004 PayPal restricted Nigerian users from receiving funds entirely, citing fraud. A 2014 partnership with First Bank of Nigeria was send-only and heavily restricted. PayPal returned in January 2026 via a partnership with Paga, allowing users to receive from 200+ countries and withdraw in naira.
details.energy_note: Twenty-two years of being able to pay and not be paid.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the $9,000 that did not arrive
details.description: One remote worker recalled losing access to a $9,000 payment in 2023 after PayPal refused to remit funds without clear reasons. Many Nigerian freelancers lost contracts outright because clients preferred PayPal and would not use anything else.
details.energy_note: Nine thousand dollars, earned, and simply not released.

details.aspect: The stated reason, and the comparison that undermines it
details.description: PayPal cited high fraud rates, compliance risk, weak national identification and banking regulation. Meanwhile Nigerian fintechs such as Flutterwave and Paystack built functioning payment systems without mass account lockouts - and PayPal's 2026 return is built on the infrastructure those companies created.
details.energy_note: Too risky to serve, and now returning on rails Nigerians built.

details.aspect: The model was selective exclusion, not absence
details.description: One characterisation: users could send but not receive, and were flagged, frozen or limited disproportionately under vague risk policies. That is worse than a clean absence, because it lets a person build a business on a rail that will drop them.
details.energy_note: Allowed to pay them. Not allowed to be paid.

details.aspect: The return does not repair the twenty years
details.description: Critics note the partnership does not fix the underlying problems, and that the businesses that failed for want of a payment method between 2004 and 2026 are not recoverable.
details.energy_note: Two decades of companies that could not take money.

issues.title: The card that stops working at the border
issues.category_name: Banking, cards and payment exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: About 120 million payment cards circulate in Nigeria and the overwhelming majority cannot be used abroad or online internationally - by design of the domestic rails and by bank-imposed ceilings.

details.aspect: The composition of the card base
details.description: Roughly 120 million active payment cards per CBN and NIBSS metrics, of which about 95% are standard naira debit cards linked to consumer naira accounts - the exact cards that faced the $20 monthly international ceiling and blanket suspensions. Many fintech-issued cards were built entirely on domestic rails with no international capability at all.
details.energy_note: A hundred and twenty million cards, and a twenty-dollar ceiling.

details.aspect: What a $20 ceiling actually forecloses
details.description: A software subscription, a conference registration, an exam fee, a domain renewal, a textbook, a visa application portal. The ceiling is below the price of participating in a professional life.
details.energy_note: Priced out of the internet by your own bank card.

details.aspect: The setting resets, silently
details.description: Many banks disable international online payments unless explicitly enabled, and the setting often resets after a few days or a number of transactions - so a card that worked last month declines at checkout with no explanation.
details.energy_note: It worked in March. It does not work in April.

details.aspect: And the merchant may have blocked the BIN anyway
details.description: Merchants and processors maintain BIN blocklists by issuing country as fraud prevention, so a fully functional card can still be declined because the merchant has decided not to accept cards from that bank.
details.energy_note: Declined by a shop, for your bank's first six digits.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the exam fee
details.description: Her professional certification exam costs $215. Her card ceiling is $20. She pays a man in a WhatsApp group 12% to put it on his UK card, sends him the naira, and trusts him, because the alternative is not sitting the exam.
details.money_note: The 12% premium on an unavoidable payment.
details.energy_note: Paying a stranger a commission to be allowed to take an exam.

issues.title: Remittance in, difficulty out
issues.category_name: Banking, cards and payment exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Money flows into Nigeria at scale and with official encouragement. Money flowing out, or being received by a Nigerian business from abroad, meets a different regime entirely.

details.aspect: The asymmetry is structural, not accidental
details.description: Inbound remittance is a foreign-exchange source and is facilitated. Outbound payment and inbound business revenue are controlled, because both touch scarce hard currency.
details.energy_note: Easy to be sent money. Hard to earn it.

details.aspect: Multiple exchange rates mean the official one costs you
details.description: Where official and parallel rates diverge, receiving through formal channels converts at the worse rate, so the compliant route is the expensive one.
details.money_note: Annual loss to the rate differential.
details.energy_note: Punished, in percentage terms, for using the legal route.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the diaspora daughter
details.description: She sends her mother money monthly from Manchester. The transfer fee is modest, the rate is not, and the difference across a year is roughly what her mother's medication costs. She has never mentioned this to her mother.
details.energy_note: A year of the exchange rate, priced in tablets.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the school fee
details.description: Her son's fees in Accra are USD 2,400 a term. Sending it through the bank converts at the official rate and requires documentation of purpose; sending it the other way is faster, cheaper and technically an offence. She has done both and only tells her husband about one of them.
details.energy_note: The legal route, and the one that works.

issues.title: Being de-risked as a category
issues.category_name: Banking, cards and payment exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Compliance departments manage country risk by declining the country. The individual customer is never assessed, and never told that is what happened.

details.aspect: Account opening, refused without reasons
details.description: Nigerian-origin customers abroad report refusals and closures with no stated ground, because stating one may constitute tipping off. There is no accusation to rebut.
details.energy_note: Declined, permanently, with no charge stated.

details.aspect: A closure follows you
details.description: Every subsequent institution sees a closed account and applies its own caution. One unexplained closure produces a pattern that then justifies itself.
details.energy_note: One closure, and then all of them.

details.aspect: Business banking is where it bites hardest
details.description: A merchant account, a payment processor, a business current account. Without these there is no company, regardless of the customers, the revenue or the product.
details.energy_note: Allowed to trade, not allowed to bank.

details.aspect: Structurally identical across these datasets
details.description: The mechanism is the same one recorded for Iranians and Palestinians: a compliance decision taken about a nationality, executed against an individual, with no route of appeal. Only the country name changes.
details.energy_note: Same paragraph, different passport.
details.notes: Cross-reference: FIN category in assets/text/iran and assets/text/palestine.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the business account
details.description: Two founders, a UK company, a signed contract with a Manchester client. The bank declines the business account. No reason is given, because giving one may constitute tipping off. They try three more banks over five months, then register the company in Estonia instead.
details.energy_note: A real company, banked in a country neither founder has seen.

details.aspect: It selects who gets to build anything
details.description: The founders who survive this are the ones with a relative abroad, a second passport, or enough capital to wait five months. The constraint does not filter for the best businesses; it filters for the best-connected ones, and then the outcome is read as a comment on Nigerian enterprise.
details.energy_note: A filter on connections, mistaken for a filter on merit.

issues.title: Being blocked for where your IP says you are
issues.category_name: Geoblocking, platforms and digital redlining
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Merchants and platforms exclude Nigeria at the network level. The block is national in scope, trivially evaded by the people it targets, and binding on everyone who is not trying to evade anything.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - removing the country from the checkout
details.description: Merchants have discussed removing countries like Nigeria from the shopping cart entirely so orders cannot be placed at all - described in forums as simple and effective, and praised as such.
details.energy_note: Not blocked from buying. Removed from the list of countries.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the published national blocklist
details.description: Publicly distributed .htaccess blocklists provide DENY rules covering Nigerian ISPs, including address blocks leased from European and US providers but reassigned to Nigeria. Coverage extends across satellite, internet cafés, DSL, cable and dialup - a block that is effectively national rather than targeted at identified bad actors.
details.energy_note: A file you can download that blocks a country.

details.aspect: The fraud-scoring logic, and the number that cuts both ways
details.description: Merchant guidance treats a billing address in one country and delivery to Africa as presumptively fraudulent. Academic work on scam geolocation found that of 965 scammer IP addresses in one Craigslist study, 50.3% were Nigerian and 37.6% were from the United States - the second figure rarely producing any equivalent country-level block.
details.energy_note: Half from Nigeria, over a third from America. One country gets blocked.

details.aspect: It fails against the people it is aimed at
details.description: Sophisticated actors route through local providers and VPNs; the block mainly removes casual fraudsters and ordinary users. The enforcement problem is acknowledged even in the merchant forums that recommend the practice.
details.energy_note: Stops the honest, not the fraudulent.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 'the invisible tax of being Nigerian'
details.description: A first-person account describes the cumulative effect: a Fiverr block with no explanation, geo-blocked learning platforms, and international clients disengaging after Lagos was mentioned - summarised as the premise that if your IP says Nigeria, you work twice as hard for half as much.
details.energy_note: Twice the work, half the rate, for a location.

details.aspect: HONEST GAP - the harm is illustrated, not quantified
details.description: No empirical study was located measuring how many legitimate Nigerian transactions are rejected, the false-positive rates of commercial fraud scoring on Nigerian traffic, or regulatory treatment of geoblocking as discrimination. The sources here are forums, a self-published blocklist and a personal essay. The mechanism is documented; the magnitude is not.
details.energy_note: Everyone can describe it. Nobody has measured it.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the course she paid for and cannot open
details.description: The certification platform accepts her card. Two weeks in, the video player returns a region error. Support explains that content licensing restricts her territory. The refund window closed on day seven.
details.energy_note: Bought it, cannot watch it, cannot return it.

issues.title: Platforms that flag you by default
issues.category_name: Geoblocking, platforms and digital redlining
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Freelance marketplaces, marketplaces and social platforms apply elevated scrutiny to Nigerian accounts, with suspension arriving before any explanation.

details.aspect: Suspension first, review later, if at all
details.description: Accounts are limited or closed pending review, with funds held. The seller has delivered the work; the platform holds the money; the appeal is a form.
details.energy_note: Work delivered, money held, nobody to call.

details.aspect: The 20-30% that never reaches the freelancer
details.description: On Upwork, Palestinian and Nigerian freelancers alike lose a further 20-30% of earnings to currency-exchange intermediaries on top of platform fees, because the standard payout rails are unavailable.
details.money_note: Annual loss to intermediaries at typical freelance income.
details.energy_note: A quarter of every invoice, to the plumbing.

details.aspect: So the ceiling is the payment method, not the skill
details.description: A business cannot scale past the rail it can be paid on. The constraint is not talent, market or capital.
details.energy_note: A company that cannot grow larger than a bank transfer.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the five-star seller
details.description: Ninety-one completed jobs, 4.9 average, two years of history. The account is restricted on a Tuesday pending identity review. She uploads the same NIN she uploaded at signup. On day thirty-one it is restored with no explanation and her ranking has reset.
details.energy_note: Two years of reputation, reset by a review.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the withdrawal threshold
details.description: The platform will only pay out to accounts in supported countries. She uses a cousin's account in Canada. In November the cousin's bank asks the cousin about the pattern of incoming payments, and the cousin, reasonably, asks her to stop.
details.energy_note: A workaround that ended with a phone call to Toronto.

issues.title: The internet costs more and works less
issues.category_name: Geoblocking, platforms and digital redlining
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Before any discrimination, the connection itself is expensive relative to income, unreliable, and dependent on the power supply in PWR-001.

details.aspect: Data is priced against a low wage
details.description: Mobile data is the primary access route and is bought in small increments, which is the most expensive way to buy anything.
details.money_note: Annual mobile data spend.
details.energy_note: Buying the internet by the handful.

details.aspect: And it needs electricity to be useful
details.description: A laptop, a router and a charged phone all depend on PWR-001. A remote job requires a power solution before it requires a skill.
details.energy_note: The job needs a generator before it needs you.

details.aspect: Which shapes what work is possible
details.description: Synchronous work - calls, live support, trading hours - requires reliability that cannot be promised, so the available remote work skews to asynchronous and lower-paid.
details.energy_note: Excluded from the jobs that need you to be reachable at two o'clock.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the interview that dropped
details.description: Second-round video interview, 14:00. NEPA goes at 13:40. The generator has fuel for ninety minutes and the inverter is at 22%. She joins from her phone on mobile data, in a stairwell, and apologises twice for the background noise.
details.energy_note: Interviewed from a stairwell, and knowing how it read.

issues.title: Kidnapping as an industry
issues.category_name: Insecurity: kidnapping, banditry and armed groups
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: What began as ideological abduction became a ransom business with a price list. It is low-risk, lucrative, and now operates across most of the country rather than one corner of it.

details.aspect: The measured volume, and why it is an undercount
details.description: Between July 2022 and June 2023, 3,620 people were abducted in 582 kidnapping cases, with about 5 billion naira - roughly $3.9 million - paid in ransoms. The real figure is higher because many families do not report, fearing reprisals.
details.money_note: Ransom, per incident, typical range.
details.energy_note: Three and a half thousand people, in twelve months, that were counted.

details.aspect: The actors are not who the headlines say
details.description: Many kidnappings are carried out by amorphous armed bandit groups with no affiliation to Boko Haram or ISWAP, whose motivations are sectarian. Treating all of it as terrorism misreads both the threat and the remedy.
details.energy_note: Not ideology. A business with a catchment area.

details.aspect: The regional map
details.description: North-east: Boko Haram and ISWAP. North-west: armed bandits using forest hideouts for kidnapping and cattle rustling. North-central: farmer-herder clashes. South-east: separatist-linked violence. Most of the country has a version.
details.energy_note: Four different threats, and a map with no blank space.

details.aspect: The ransom economy sets a price on a person
details.description: Families sell land, vehicles and businesses, or borrow at punitive rates, against a deadline. The asset base of a household can be destroyed by a single successful abduction regardless of the outcome.
details.energy_note: A family's entire capital, converted to cash, in four days.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the road to Kaduna
details.description: She stops travelling that road by car. The flight costs eleven times as much and she takes it, four times a year, which is a meaningful fraction of her salary. Her mother, who cannot afford the flight, takes the road.
details.energy_note: Buying safety by the seat, for the people who can.

details.aspect: It reorganises where people will live and work
details.description: Jobs not taken, farms not worked, schools not attended, roads not used after dark. The economic geography of a country is rewritten by a crime statistic.
details.energy_note: A map of where you are willing to be.

issues.title: Taking the schoolchildren
issues.category_name: Insecurity: kidnapping, banditry and armed groups
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Mass school abduction became a repeatable tactic after 2014. The specific consequence is that education itself becomes a risk calculation, and it is calculated differently for daughters.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Chibok, 14 April 2014
details.description: 276 schoolgirls were taken from Government Girls Secondary School in Chibok, Borno State. 82 escaped on their own, 103 were released in small groups between 2016 and 2017 in exchange for prisoners, and at least 91 remain in captivity or their fate is unknown.
details.time_note: Twelve years, for those not returned.
details.energy_note: Ninety-one girls, still unaccounted for.

details.aspect: And it did not stop
details.description: Amnesty has documented at least 17 mass school abductions since 2014 involving more than 1,700 children; ICIR counted 26 major school attacks between April 2014 and May 2026 with at least 2,416 students abducted. In November 2025 some 400 people were kidnapped including more than 300 schoolchildren in two assaults, prompting a UN warning of a surge in mass abductions.
details.energy_note: Seventeen Chiboks, and counting.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a billion naira for 287 children
details.description: ANSARU militants abducted 287 students and staff from a Kaduna State school and demanded 1 billion naira, around US$600,000.
details.energy_note: A price quoted, per school.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the camps are targets too
details.description: In 2024 Boko Haram abducted over 400 people, mainly women and schoolchildren, from an internally displaced people's camp in Borno State - taking people who had already fled once.
details.energy_note: Displaced to safety, and taken from there.

details.aspect: The protection scheme did not arrive
details.description: Nigeria endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration after Chibok. HRW reported the initiative faced problems and declining momentum with little or no progress in fortifying schools; in 2021 the then-Senate president said after an investigation into fund use that it was designed to fail without a national policy and strategy.
details.energy_note: A declaration signed, and the schools unchanged.

details.aspect: Girls are withdrawn first
details.description: Where a household reduces risk by removing a child from school, the daughter goes before the son - which converts an act of violence into a permanent educational gap that appears in the statistics decades later.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings effect of withdrawal.
details.energy_note: Pulled out for her safety, and the cost is the rest of her life.
details.notes: Feeds directly into EDU-002 and WRK-002.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the boarding school decision
details.description: The good secondary school is boarding, four hours away, and in a state that was in the news in March. The day school nearby is weaker and she will pass fewer subjects. Her parents choose the day school and never discuss it again.
details.energy_note: A worse education, chosen deliberately, for a good reason.

issues.title: Being displaced inside your own country
issues.category_name: Insecurity: kidnapping, banditry and armed groups
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
