issues.summary: Millions have left home without crossing a border, which means no refugee status, no agency mandate, and frequently no camp - just another poor village absorbing people it cannot feed.

details.aspect: The herder-farmer displacement, by the numbers
details.description: From January 2015 to February 2017 at least 62,000 people were displaced in Kaduna, Benue and Plateau - and with no IDP camps available most sheltered in other poor rural communities. An estimated 300,000 fled after the January 2018 escalation, and by 2025 close to 500,000 people in Benue had been displaced.
details.energy_note: Half a million people, in one state, with nowhere organised to go.

details.aspect: The scale of the conflict producing it
details.description: Violence has affected more than 20 states, particularly Benue, Plateau, Taraba, Adamawa, Kaduna, Kwara, Borno and Zamfara. In 2016 one count put herder-related deaths at 1,425 against 1,240 attributed to Boko Haram in the same period.
details.energy_note: Deadlier than the insurgency, in the year nobody reported it.

details.aspect: Hosting is unfunded and has a half-life
details.description: Displaced families absorbed by relatives strain households that were already poor. The first month is solidarity; by the third the food, space and goodwill are gone, and nobody can say so.
details.energy_note: A welcome you can feel expiring.

details.aspect: The land does not wait
details.description: Farmland not worked for a season is farmland claimed, degraded or occupied. Displacement that is temporary in intention becomes permanent through the agricultural calendar.
details.energy_note: One missed planting season, and it is not yours.

details.aspect: Women's work is where the strain lands
details.description: Water, fuel, food and childcare in an unfamiliar place with no infrastructure are performed by women, and the hours are counted as leisure in every time-use survey.
details.time_note: Days per year of additional unpaid logistics.
details.energy_note: Four extra hours a day, uncounted.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Benue displacement, by the numbers
details.description: From January 2015 to February 2017 at least 62,000 people were displaced in Kaduna, Benue and Plateau, and with no IDP camps available most sheltered in other poor rural communities. An estimated 300,000 fled after the January 2018 escalation. By 2025 close to 500,000 people in Benue had been displaced, most from villages now considered too dangerous to return to.
details.energy_note: Half a million people, in one state, and no camps.

issues.title: The security you have to buy
issues.category_name: Insecurity: kidnapping, banditry and armed groups
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Where the state does not provide protection, households and businesses purchase it - which makes safety an income-tiered product and leaves everyone else with the risk.

details.aspect: The private layer
details.description: Gates, guards, estate fees, vigilante contributions, dogs, bars on windows. A recurring cost that replaces a public service.
details.money_note: Annual household security spend.
details.energy_note: Paying, monthly, for something taxes were meant to cover.

details.aspect: Communities formed militias for the same reason
details.description: Several farmer and herder communities have formed armed groups, allegedly in response to a lack of government protection - which raises the ambient level of weaponry and the next round of casualties.
details.energy_note: Arming yourself, because nobody came.

details.aspect: Women pay a movement tax instead of a money one
details.description: Where cash is not available, the security adaptation is restriction: not travelling after dark, not going alone, not taking that road. It costs opportunity rather than naira and nobody records it.
details.energy_note: A curfew nobody announced and everybody keeps.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the estate levy
details.description: NGN 15,000 a month for the gate, the guards and the generator for the street lights. It is not optional in any meaningful sense and it is not a tax, so it appears in no measure of what she pays for public services.
details.energy_note: A private tax, monthly, for a public good.

issues.title: The checkpoint that wants twenty naira
issues.category_name: Police, extortion and what happened at Lekki
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Routine police extortion is a small, constant, unavoidable levy on movement, and refusing it is more expensive than paying.

details.aspect: It is priced to be paid
details.description: The demand is set below the value of the time and risk of refusing. That is what makes it sustainable and what makes it universal.
details.money_note: Annual, in small repeated payments.
details.energy_note: Cheaper to pay than to argue, every time, by design.

details.aspect: Refusal escalates immediately
details.description: A vehicle search, a manufactured infraction, a trip to the station, a day gone. The escalation path is known to everyone, which is why it rarely has to be used.
details.energy_note: Standing on principle costs you a working day.

details.aspect: Young men and visible earners are targeted
details.description: A laptop, a good phone, dreadlocks, a nice car. Markers of a young person doing well function as selection criteria, which is the SARS pattern in POL-002 in its everyday form.
details.energy_note: Stopped for owning a laptop.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the airport run
details.description: Four stops between Ikeja and the terminal. Two hundred naira, two hundred, one hundred, and one who waves them through. She has budgeted for this. Her visiting cousin from Manchester has not, and argues at the second one, and they miss check-in by nine minutes.
details.energy_note: A flight missed by someone who did not know the tariff.

issues.title: What happened at Lekki
issues.category_name: Police, extortion and what happened at Lekki
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: The clearest documented case of the state using lethal force on its own unarmed citizens in this dataset - established by a judicial panel, denied by the government, and unpunished.

details.aspect: What preceded it
details.description: Nationwide #EndSARS protests began on 8 October 2020 against brutality by the Special Anti-Robbery Squad, days after a widely distributed video showed SARS officers dragging two men from a hotel and shooting one outside.
details.energy_note: A video on a Saturday, and a country in the street by Thursday.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the panel's finding
details.description: The Justice Doris Okuwobi-led judicial panel submitted a 309-page report finding at least 48 protesters shot dead, injured or assaulted at the Lekki Toll Gate on 20 October 2020, that soldiers of the 65 Battalion fired blank and live rounds at demonstrators, and that the conduct 'could, in context, be described as a massacre'. It found the Army worsened it by refusing to allow ambulances to reach victims.
details.energy_note: A judicial panel used the word massacre.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the official response
details.description: The army said its officers fired only blanks. On the first anniversary the Information Minister said the 'only massacre recorded was in the social media'. The Lagos state government's White Paper rejected the panel's finding on the number killed.
details.energy_note: A 309-page finding, and a minister saying it happened on Twitter.

details.aspect: Amnesty's parallel finding
details.description: Amnesty International investigated on the ground the following day and confirmed at least 12 peaceful protesters killed at Lekki and Alausa, from eyewitnesses, video and hospital records.
details.energy_note: Two independent findings, one denial.

details.aspect: The effect on whether anyone protests again
details.description: The lesson available to a young Nigerian is that a peaceful mass movement produced a panel, a report, a denial and no prosecutions. Political participation is priced accordingly.
details.energy_note: It was investigated, established, and nothing followed.

details.aspect: And it accelerated the leaving
details.description: The japa wave in HLT-002 is frequently dated by the people in it to October 2020 rather than to any economic figure.
details.energy_note: A lot of people decided to leave that week.

issues.title: Reporting a crime as a woman
issues.category_name: Police, extortion and what happened at Lekki
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: The institution that would record a sexual or domestic offence is frequently the one that dissuades, mocks, charges a fee, or suggests the family settle it.

details.aspect: The first obstacle is the counter
details.description: Reports are commonly discouraged as family matters, met with demands for money to open a case or fuel a vehicle, or handled by officers who tell the complainant to reconsider.
details.energy_note: Paying, to have a crime against you written down.

details.aspect: Medical evidence requires money and speed
details.description: A medical report requires a hospital, a fee, and attendance before the evidence degrades - all within hours, at the worst possible moment, usually without transport.
details.energy_note: Evidence with a deadline, and a fee, on the same night.

details.aspect: Settlement out of court is the default outcome
details.description: Family mediation, an apology, a payment, sometimes a marriage. The case ends without a record, which is why conviction figures are so low and why the low figures are then cited as evidence the offences are rare.
details.energy_note: Resolved, unrecorded, and then counted as not having happened.

details.aspect: The law exists and lives in a different building
details.description: VAPP 2015 expanded the definition of rape and criminalised harmful widowhood practices. Kano has not enacted it; implementation is uneven across states; and in August 2024 a bill to repeal it reached second reading in the Senate.
details.energy_note: A good law, unevenly adopted, and nearly repealed.
details.notes: See WOM-001 for the full legislative picture.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the station at 11pm
details.description: The officer asks whether she wants to 'spoil the man's life' and suggests she return in the morning with her uncle. She returns in the morning with her uncle. The matter is settled between the families by the following Sunday and no report is ever written.
details.energy_note: Resolved on Sunday, recorded nowhere.

issues.title: The grid that goes off, nationally
issues.category_name: Electricity, fuel and the generator economy
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Not outages in the ordinary sense. The national grid collapses entirely, repeatedly, and everything downstream of electricity is built around the assumption that it will.

details.aspect: Total collapse is a recurring event
details.description: Nigeria suffered a total blackout on 14 September 2023 when the national grid collapsed, with distribution companies citing system failure. The grid collapsed twelve times in the first half of 2024 alone, with further failures into 2026.
details.energy_note: The whole country's electricity, off, twelve times in six months.

details.aspect: The outage hours, against the regional average
details.description: Sub-Saharan outages averaged 56 hours per month in 2024; Nigeria's industrial clusters regularly exceed 200 hours.
details.energy_note: Two hundred hours a month without power, in the industrial areas.

details.aspect: So the generator is the actual grid
details.description: A dense ecosystem of distributors with nationwide financing, parts and maintenance networks sustains generator dependence. Every outage drives further generator investment, and fuel subsidies long made that artificially competitive.
details.money_note: Annual generator purchase, fuel and maintenance.
details.energy_note: A second, private, petrol-powered national grid.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - fifty-seven thousand naira a week, for a barber
details.description: One Lagos barber described spending N57,000 on generator fuel in a single week while unable to raise haircut prices without losing customers - the squeeze in its simplest form.
details.energy_note: A week's fuel, and the same price per haircut.

details.aspect: Women's unpaid work absorbs the schedule
details.description: Cooking, laundry, water pumping, phone charging and children's homework are scheduled around whenever the power is on, including at night. The household manager does the absorbing.
details.time_note: Days per year of rescheduled domestic labour.
details.energy_note: Doing the washing at 2am because that is when it came on.

details.aspect: It sets a ceiling on which industries can exist
details.description: No cold chain, no reliable manufacturing, no data centre, no synchronous remote work at scale. The power schedule is an industrial policy nobody wrote.
details.energy_note: Whole sectors, ruled out by a generator.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the freezer
details.description: She sells frozen fish. Six hours of grid power a day and a generator that costs NGN 9,000 a day to run against a margin that does not support it. In August she loses a full freezer and with it the working capital for the month.
details.energy_note: A business model destroyed by a power schedule.

details.aspect: A generation grows up scheduling around it
details.description: Children raised on the power schedule study when the light is on rather than when they are able to concentrate, charge everything the moment it returns, and carry the habit into countries where it is unnecessary. It reads there as anxiety.
details.energy_note: Charging everything at once, in a country where you needn't.

issues.title: Paying for darkness
issues.category_name: Electricity, fuel and the generator economy
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: More than half of registered electricity customers have no meter, so they are billed by estimate - and the estimates are systematically wrong in one direction.

details.aspect: The metering gap
details.description: As of 31 December 2024 only 6,288,642 of 13,503,342 registered customers were metered - 46.57%. The national meter deficit is around seven million, and over 72% of distribution companies failed to meet approved metering thresholds.
details.energy_note: Over half the country billed for a quantity nobody measured.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - two million overbilled, and the refund
details.description: More than two million consumers were overbilled in 2024, producing credit adjustments totalling N105.05 billion. The regulator tied the rise in overbilling to implementation of the Band A tariff regime.
details.money_note: Per household, annual overbilling before adjustment.
details.energy_note: A hundred and five billion naira, billed for nothing.

details.aspect: Band A, and the 162% expansion
details.description: Band A feeders - those expected to deliver 20 hours of daily electricity at N225 per kWh, the highest rate - expanded from 481 in April 2024 to 1,261 by April 2025, a 162% surge, despite widespread complaints of unreliable supply. Reported charge differences ran as high as 500%.
details.energy_note: Reclassified upward, and the supply did not change.

details.aspect: The meter is the remedy and is withheld
details.description: Metered customers can only be billed more if more power is supplied, which is precisely why estimated billing persists. Consumers below Band B report erratic supply and describe the arrangement as exploitation.
details.energy_note: The fix exists, costs little, and is not installed.

details.aspect: Disputing it costs a fortnight
details.description: The escalation path requires logging actual daily supply hours for at least two weeks, then a formal band review request, then 30 days, then the regulator. The process is longer than the billing cycle it disputes.
details.energy_note: Two weeks of homework to contest one bill.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the landlady's arithmetic
details.description: Six tenants, one estimated bill, no meter. She divides it six ways. Two tenants have air conditioners and four do not, and the four know it, and this is the reason two of them are leaving.
details.energy_note: An unmeasured bill, splitting a house.

issues.title: The morning the fuel price doubled
issues.category_name: Inflation, subsidy removal and the cost of an ordinary month
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: On 29 May 2023 the fuel subsidy was removed in a sentence, and the price of moving anything - people, food, goods - repriced within weeks.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the announcement and the number
details.description: Petrol was 219.03 naira per litre before removal. A year later the average retail price had more than doubled to 655.48 naira - a 199.26% increase in twelve months. Daily consumption fell from about 66.9 million litres to 48.43 million.
details.energy_note: Two hundred and nineteen naira, then six hundred and fifty-five.

details.aspect: Commuting rose by nearly 300%
details.description: Transport costs surged by close to 300%, with direct knock-on effects on the cost of essential food commodities, because in Nigeria food price is largely a transport price.
details.money_note: Annual additional commuting cost.
details.energy_note: The bus to work, tripled.

details.aspect: Inflation followed and kept going
details.description: Headline inflation rose from 22.41% in May 2023 to 22.79% in June, then 31.70% by February 2024 and 34.19% by June 2024.
details.energy_note: A third of the value of everything, in a year.

details.aspect: The World Bank's estimate of who it pushed under
details.description: The World Bank warned that if conditions persisted an additional 4 million citizens would likely join the 133 million already in multidimensional poverty.
details.energy_note: Four million more, on top of a hundred and thirty-three.

details.aspect: The counter-argument, stated fairly
details.description: The subsidy had become fiscally unsustainable at over N1 trillion annually and was associated with corruption and smuggling. Removal created fiscal space, curtailed smuggling and accelerated reform. Both things are true; only one of them is experienced at a market stall.
details.energy_note: A defensible policy, paid for by people with no margin.

details.aspect: Palliatives did not reach the gap
details.description: Cash transfers and a compressed-natural-gas initiative were introduced; critics describe them as insufficient and poorly targeted, which is the ordinary fate of a transfer programme in a country with an incomplete identity system.
details.energy_note: Compensation that requires a database nobody finished.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the danfo fare
details.description: The fare to her shop went from NGN 300 to NGN 900 across eight months. Her margin did not move. By the fourth month she is walking part of it; by the sixth she is opening four days a week instead of six.
details.energy_note: A business shrunk by the cost of getting to it.

issues.title: Running a household at 34% inflation
issues.category_name: Inflation, subsidy removal and the cost of an ordinary month
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: The management of a shrinking budget against rising prices is daily, skilled, unpaid work, and it is overwhelmingly done by women.

details.aspect: Substitution down the quality ladder
details.description: The same meal, made from cheaper components, then fewer components, then fewer meals. The adjustment is continuous and invisible from outside the household.
details.energy_note: The same pot, with less in it, every month.

details.aspect: Buying small is the expensive way to buy
details.description: Sachet economics - a cup of rice, a sachet of oil, a hundred naira of recharge. Unit costs are highest for those with the least, which is a poverty premium paid daily.
details.money_note: Annual poverty premium from small-quantity purchasing.
details.energy_note: Charged more per gram, for having less cash.

details.aspect: School fees are the first casualty and the last admitted
details.description: Fees, uniforms, books and exam registrations are lumpy costs in a month with no slack, and the decision to defer them is made quietly and usually about a daughter first.
details.energy_note: A term skipped, and nobody outside the house is told.

details.aspect: The cognitive load is the hidden cost
details.description: Continuous arithmetic about prices, credit, who is owed, what can wait. It occupies the same attention that would go to work or study, which is the mechanism in PSY-004.
details.energy_note: A calculator running in your head, all day, for years.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the pot in August
details.description: In January the stew had beef twice a week. By April it is beef on Sundays. By August it is beef when someone is visiting. Nobody in the house has been told that anything changed, and the children have stopped asking.
details.energy_note: The same pot, quietly emptier, month by month.

details.aspect: Managing it well is what conceals it
details.description: The better she is at absorbing the shortfall, the less anyone else in the household registers that there is one - so competence at this work guarantees that it goes unrecognised, and the recognition is what would get her help.
details.energy_note: Rewarded for hiding it, and therefore never helped.

issues.title: Being paid in a currency that is leaving
issues.category_name: Inflation, subsidy removal and the cost of an ordinary month
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Naira earnings against dollar-denominated costs - school fees abroad, software, medical treatment, imported goods - means a salary that falls in real terms without anyone cutting it.

details.aspect: Effort and outcome decouple
details.description: A salary negotiated in one year buys substantially less by the next without anything happening. That is the precondition for the planning collapse in PSY-003.
details.energy_note: Working harder, and having less, reliably.

details.aspect: Saving in naira is a choice to lose money
details.description: Households convert to goods, dollars or property where they can. The resulting absence of formal savings is then read abroad as financial illiteracy.
details.energy_note: Punished for not saving in a currency that eats itself.

details.aspect: Which makes emigration the dominant financial strategy
details.description: When domestic accumulation does not work, converting labour into foreign currency becomes the only reliable plan - which is japa, stated as arithmetic rather than aspiration.
details.energy_note: Leaving, as a savings product.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the savings for the shop
details.description: She saved NGN 2.1 million over four years for a shop front in Surulere. By the time she had it, the same shop front cost NGN 5.4 million. She had not spent a naira of it and had lost most of it.
details.energy_note: Four years of discipline, and the goalposts moved further than she walked.

issues.title: A health system with a third of its doctors licensed elsewhere
issues.category_name: The health system, and the people who left it
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Nigeria trains health workers and then loses them, at a rate that has converted a staffing problem into a structural one.

details.aspect: The workforce that is left
details.description: Nigeria's health minister has stated there are about 300,000 health professionals in the country across all cadres, with 85,000-90,000 registered doctors but only 55,000 licensed and practising in-country.
details.energy_note: Ninety thousand doctors on the register. Fifty-five thousand in the country.

details.aspect: What that means at the point of care
details.description: Remaining practitioners face overwork and burnout, hospitals lack specialists in surgery, anaesthesia and paediatrics, and some rural communities have no doctor at all.
details.energy_note: A community with no doctor, as an ordinary fact.

details.aspect: Out-of-pocket is the payment model
details.description: Without broad insurance coverage, treatment is bought at the point of need in cash, which means the sequence is: fall ill, find money, then be treated - and the finding-money step is where people die.
details.energy_note: The deposit before the drip.

details.aspect: Which makes illness a household financial event
details.description: Assets sold, loans taken, school fees diverted. A single serious diagnosis can reset a family's economic position permanently.
details.energy_note: One diagnosis, and the family is poor again.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the deposit
details.description: Her father is admitted at 21:00. The ward will not begin until N180,000 is paid. She calls four people between 21:00 and 01:40 and raises N145,000. The remaining N35,000 arrives at 07:15 from her brother in Ontario.
details.energy_note: Ten hours of phone calls, standing in a corridor.

issues.title: Japa: the exit as a national event
issues.category_name: The health system, and the people who left it
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Emigration of skilled workers is not a trickle or an aspiration. It is measurable in the destination countries' own registration data, and the health sector is where it is most visible.

details.aspect: The nurses
details.description: About 16,000 Nigerian nurses migrated to the UK in 2025 alone, taking the five-year total to around 57,000. Peer-reviewed work found about 42,000 nurses left Nigeria in 2022-2024, the largest sub-Saharan African contribution to the NHS nursing workforce in Great Britain.
details.energy_note: Fifty-seven thousand nurses, in five years, to one country.

details.aspect: The doctors
details.description: Between 2021 and 2024, 8,560 Nigerian doctors registered with the UK's General Medical Council - 39% of all international registrations - while another 2,454 went to the US, Canada and Australia. By late 2023, 12,198 Nigerian-trained doctors were licensed in the UK.
details.energy_note: Thirty-nine per cent of every foreign doctor the UK registered.

details.aspect: The red list that does not stop it
details.description: Nigeria is among 54 countries the UK lists as not to be actively recruited from, on WHO criteria - a UHC Service Coverage Index below 50 and health worker density below the global median of 48.6 per 10,000. The code bars active recruitment, not individual applications, which is why the migration continued regardless.
details.energy_note: Listed as too fragile to recruit from, and recruited from anyway.

details.aspect: The intention data, which predicts the rest
details.description: A 2022 study of emigration intentions among skilled health workers found nurses (72%) and doctors (55%) the most likely to migrate. The pipeline is not closing.
details.energy_note: Seven in ten nurses intending to go.

details.aspect: The proposed remedy is a bond on a person
details.description: A push for mandatory five-year national service for doctors before full licensure abroad would solve the outflow by removing the right to leave, which is a different kind of problem.
details.energy_note: Fixing the exit by closing the door.

details.aspect: Those who stay carry the gap
details.description: The nurse who did not leave works the ward the four who left used to staff. Her burnout is the mechanism by which the next four decide.
details.energy_note: Each departure makes the next one more likely.

details.aspect: And the training was paid for domestically
details.description: Nigeria bears the cost of educating the workforce; the destination country receives a trained professional at no training cost. It is a subsidy flowing from a poor health system to rich ones.
details.money_note: Public cost of training one doctor, transferred abroad.
details.energy_note: A poor country, subsidising rich countries' hospitals.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the GMC registrations
details.description: Between 2021 and 2024, 8,560 Nigerian doctors registered with the UK's General Medical Council - 39% of all international registrations - while 2,454 more went to the US, Canada and Australia. By late 2023, 12,198 Nigerian-trained doctors were licensed in the UK, putting Nigeria on track to pass Pakistan as the second-largest source of foreign-trained doctors there after India.
details.energy_note: Thirty-nine per cent of every foreign doctor the UK registered.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the ward at 3am
details.description: She is the only doctor on the floor. Four of the six who trained with her are in Britain. She is not angry with them; she has the application half-finished on her own laptop and has had it there for eleven months.
details.energy_note: Covering for the four who left, with her own form half-typed.

issues.title: Being treated abroad, and being suspected there
issues.category_name: The health system, and the people who left it
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Nigerian nationality, passport or origin, anywhere
issues.summary: Nigerian patients and Nigerian-trained clinicians abroad both encounter a presumption - of health tourism in one direction, of inadequate training in the other.

details.aspect: The maternity-tourism presumption
details.description: A pregnant Nigerian traveller is assessed against an assumption about why she is travelling, regardless of her actual purpose - which makes a visa harder and a border harder at exactly the point in life when travel is least comfortable.
details.energy_note: Interrogated at a border while visibly pregnant.

details.aspect: Requalification for clinicians
details.description: Nigerian-trained doctors and nurses face examinations, supervised practice and language testing before working at their level - years in which they work below their training and are paid accordingly.
details.energy_note: A consultant, working as a junior, for three years.

details.aspect: And the accent is assessed as competence
details.description: Patients and colleagues read a Nigerian accent as a proxy for training quality. The clinician learns to speak differently, which is unpaid work performed during a shift.
details.energy_note: Flattening your own voice, for eight hours a day.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the nurse who is 'not yet' a nurse
details.description: Fourteen years on a Lagos ward. In the UK she is a healthcare assistant for nineteen months while her registration proceeds, doing much of the same work, at a third of the pay, being trained by people she has more experience than.
details.energy_note: Fourteen years of experience, re-entered at the bottom.

issues.title: One of the most dangerous places in the world to give birth
issues.category_name: Maternal health, obstructed labour and fistula
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Nigeria carries a share of global maternal deaths far out of proportion to its population, and the northern ratio is several times the national one.

details.aspect: The share of the world's maternal deaths
details.description: Estimates vary by source and year: roughly 40,000 pregnancy-related deaths annually, about 14% of the global total; a WHO-based figure puts it at 58,000, 19.1% of 303,000. Nigeria is among the top six countries contributing more than half of all global maternal deaths.
details.energy_note: One country, a seventh to a fifth of all maternal deaths on earth.

details.aspect: The ratio, and the north
details.description: A maternal mortality ratio of 512 per 100,000 live births nationally, and over 1,000 per 100,000 in northern Nigeria. Maternal deaths account for roughly a third of all deaths among women of reproductive age.
details.energy_note: A third of all deaths of women of childbearing age.

details.aspect: Four an hour
details.description: Nigeria's own national framework put it at 4 maternal deaths per hour, 90 per day, 2,800 per month - about 34,000 annually - with at least 30 women suffering short- or long-term morbidity for every death.
details.energy_note: Four an hour, ninety a day, every day.

details.aspect: Only 43% of births have a skilled attendant
details.description: Which is the single most modifiable number in this entire category, and the one that determines whether an obstructed labour becomes a caesarean or becomes MAT-002.
details.energy_note: More than half of births, with nobody trained present.

details.aspect: The delays are geographic and financial before they are clinical
details.description: Deciding to seek care, reaching a facility, and receiving care on arrival. The first is about money and permission, the second about roads and transport, the third about staffing and the deposit in HLT-001.
details.energy_note: Three delays, and the clinical one is last.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the night before the market day
details.description: Labour starts at 23:00. The nearest facility with a theatre is 40km on a road nobody drives after dark. The traditional birth attendant is eleven minutes away. They wait for morning. It is the decision that most families in that village make, and it is usually right.
details.energy_note: Waiting for daylight, and usually being correct.

issues.title: Obstetric fistula: the injury of waiting too long
issues.category_name: Maternal health, obstructed labour and fistula
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Prolonged obstructed labour without a caesarean produces an injury that is preventable, repairable, and in Nigeria enormously common - and it ends the woman's social life as reliably as it damages her body.

details.aspect: Nigeria's share
details.description: Nigeria accounts for around 40% of obstetric fistula cases worldwide. Of roughly 2 million women globally living with unrepaired vesico-vaginal fistula, about half of the developing-world total were from Nigeria. Prevalence is 3.2 per 1,000 births with an estimated 13,000 new cases annually.
details.energy_note: Forty per cent of the world's cases, in one country.

details.aspect: The backlog, expressed in years
details.description: At current repair rates the backlog of unrepaired cases could take about 83 years to clear. UNICEF has put the number of Nigerian women living with fistula at 400,000 to 800,000; a recent modelling study gives a much lower 45,166.
details.time_note: Years of living with it, pending a repair queue of decades.
details.energy_note: An eighty-three year waiting list.
details.notes: The spread between 45,166 and 400,000-800,000 reflects genuine measurement difficulty, not carelessness. Both are recorded.

details.aspect: The mechanism
details.description: 80-95% of cases occur when a young woman experiences prolonged obstructed labour without access to a caesarean - the pelvis too small, the head too large, or the baby badly positioned. She may labour five days or more; the baby usually dies; the survivor is left with extensive tissue damage.
details.energy_note: Five days in labour, and the injury is the survival.

details.aspect: It is a child-marriage injury as much as an obstetric one
details.description: A small pelvis is a young pelvis. The states with the highest child marriage rates in WOM-003 are the states with the highest fistula burden, and the causal chain between them is not disputed.
details.energy_note: Married at fourteen, in obstructed labour at fifteen.

details.aspect: The social consequence exceeds the medical one
details.description: Continuous incontinence leads to abandonment by husbands, exclusion from gatherings, and isolation - so the woman loses the household income and the support network at the same moment she acquires a condition requiring both.
details.energy_note: Divorced, excluded, and leaking, all from one labour.

details.aspect: The repair exists and is cheap
details.description: Fistula repair is a well-established surgical procedure with high success rates. The obstacles are the number of surgeons, the distance to them, and knowing the repair exists at all.
details.money_note: Typical repair cost where available.
details.energy_note: Fixable, for a few hundred dollars, and mostly not fixed.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the woman in the back room
details.description: She was married at 15 and laboured for four days at 16. She is 34. She has lived in her brother's compound for eighteen years, does not attend the mosque, and has never been told the word for what happened to her or that there is an operation.
details.energy_note: Eighteen years, for want of being told it was repairable.

issues.title: Deciding whether to have a child at all
issues.category_name: Maternal health, obstructed labour and fistula
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Contraception, spacing and the number of pregnancies are frequently not the woman's decision to make, which converts every other maternal risk into a recurring one.

details.aspect: Spacing is what reduces risk, and requires agreement
details.description: Short inter-pregnancy intervals raise maternal and neonatal risk. Achieving longer ones requires either a partner's cooperation or covert use.
details.energy_note: A medical decision requiring somebody else's consent.

details.aspect: Covert use is common and is its own risk
details.description: Injectables and implants are chosen partly because they are undetectable. The clinical choice is being made on grounds of concealment rather than suitability.
details.energy_note: Choosing the method he cannot find.

details.aspect: Each pregnancy re-runs MAT-001
details.description: Where family size is high and skilled attendance is at 43%, the cumulative lifetime risk of maternal death is the per-birth risk compounded across births.
details.energy_note: The same dice, thrown six times.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the implant appointment
details.description: She tells him she is going to the market. The clinic is forty minutes the other way. She is back before four with vegetables she bought on the way home so the story holds.
details.energy_note: A covert operation, to space her own children.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the fifth pregnancy
details.description: She is thirty-one. The fourth delivery was a haemorrhage and the doctor at Katsina said plainly that another would be dangerous. Her husband's family have been clear that the two boys are not enough. She has not told anyone she is pregnant.
details.energy_note: A medical warning, overruled by a household.

issues.title: The cost of a delivery, in cash, on the night
issues.category_name: Maternal health, obstructed labour and fistula
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Facility delivery is priced and paid at the point of use, which makes the safest option the one that requires money to be available at 2am.

details.aspect: Deposits, consumables and the caesarean surcharge
details.description: Registration, gloves, drugs, blood, and a substantially higher price for surgical delivery - payable before or during, in a system where the decision to operate is the emergency.
details.energy_note: The operation that saves you has a price on the door.

details.aspect: Which is why home delivery is chosen by people who know the risk
details.description: The choice is not ignorance. It is a household with N4,000 and a facility that requires N60,000, making a rational decision with bad options.
details.energy_note: Not uninformed. Unfunded.

details.aspect: And detention for unpaid bills happens
details.description: Women and newborns held in facilities until bills are settled is a documented practice in several low-income health systems, and it deters the next woman from attending at all.
details.energy_note: Kept in the ward until somebody pays for you.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - kept until somebody pays
details.description: She delivered on the Friday. The bill is NGN 210,000 and her husband has raised NGN 130,000. On the Tuesday she and the baby are still on the ward, not being treated, because the ward will not discharge until it is settled. She is occupying a bed that the next woman needs.
details.energy_note: Four extra days in hospital, for want of the balance.

issues.title: The bills that were rejected
issues.category_name: Women's legal status: marriage, inheritance, the bills that failed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Nigeria's legislature has repeatedly declined to pass gender equality provisions. The refusals are recent, recorded, and are the reason several other issues in this dataset have no remedy.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the five bills, 2 March 2022
details.description: Hundreds of Nigerian women protested at the National Assembly after five bills were rejected: on citizenship, reserved parliamentary seats, affirmative action, and indigeneship - the last of which would have allowed women to become natives of their husbands' states.
details.energy_note: Five bills, one morning, all rejected.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the GEO Bill, twice
details.description: The Senate rejected the Gender and Equal Opportunities Bill on 15 December 2021 for the second time, having first been presented in 2016. Male lawmakers argued the Constitution already upholds women's rights. The bill also sought to protect widows' rights and discourage gender discrimination.
details.energy_note: Rejected twice, on the grounds that it was unnecessary.

details.aspect: VAPP exists and is federal in a federal country
details.description: The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015 is the most comprehensive legislation on violence against women - covering domestic violence, rape, FGM/C and child marriage - but as a federal law it is directly effective only in the Federal Capital Territory. States must domesticate it. Kano has not.
details.energy_note: A national law that stops at the edge of Abuja.

details.aspect: And it was nearly repealed
details.description: In August 2024 a bill to repeal the VAPP Act advanced to second reading in the Senate, drawing opposition from women's rights groups.
details.energy_note: Nine years old, and already at second reading for repeal.

details.aspect: The pattern is what matters, not any single vote
details.description: Each refusal is individually explicable. Together they describe a legislature that has declined, repeatedly and recently, to alter the position of women in law - which is why the remedies referenced elsewhere in this dataset keep being customary rather than statutory.
details.energy_note: Not one decision. A consistent answer.

issues.title: Being an indigene of nowhere
issues.category_name: Women's legal status: marriage, inheritance, the bills that failed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Indigeneship determines access to scholarships, state employment, quotas and land. It follows birth, not marriage - so a married woman is frequently treated as belonging to neither state.

details.aspect: The gap
details.description: She is no longer treated as an indigene of her birth state because she has married out, and not accepted as an indigene of her husband's state because she was not born there. Neither position is written down.
details.energy_note: From two states, and claimed by neither.

details.aspect: It was one of the five rejected bills
details.description: The indigeneship bill in WOM-001 would have allowed women to become natives of their husbands' states. It was rejected on 2 March 2022.
details.energy_note: The fix was proposed, voted on, and refused.

details.aspect: What it costs in practice
details.description: State scholarships, civil service quotas, subsidised schooling, land allocation and political candidacy all key off indigeneship certificates.
details.energy_note: Excluded from the state's own provision, by marrying.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the scholarship form
details.description: The state bursary requires an indigeneship certificate from the local government. Hers says her father's LGA. The registrar says she should apply through her husband's. Her husband's LGA says she is not from there. The deadline is Friday.
details.energy_note: Two councils, one form, no certificate.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the civil service quota
details.description: The federal character quota allocates the post by state of origin. Her file says Anambra, from her father. She has lived in Kaduna for nineteen years and her children were born there. She competes for the Anambra allocation against people who live there and know the panel.
details.energy_note: Competing for a place in a state she left at six.

issues.title: Married before eighteen
issues.category_name: Women's legal status: marriage, inheritance, the bills that failed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: A third of Nigerian girls marry before 18, and in several northern states it is nearly two thirds. The constitutional provision that would have settled the age contains a clause that undoes it.

details.aspect: The national and state figures
details.description: 33% of girls marry before 18 and about 11% before 15. By state: Jigawa 63%, Zamfara 63%, Sokoto 61%, Katsina 61%. A 2026 study reports 80% in northern Nigeria, with marriage rates of 86% among adolescent girls in control communities.
details.energy_note: Nearly two in three girls, in four states.

details.aspect: Who it happens to
details.description: 48% in rural areas against 16% urban. 67% in the poorest wealth quintile against 6% in the richest. 66.7% of women with no formal education against 13% of those who completed higher education.
details.energy_note: Eleven times more likely if you are poor.

details.aspect: The constitutional clause
details.description: Section 29(4) of the 1999 Constitution sets the age of maturity at 18, but section 29(4)(b) provides that a girl child reaches maturity on marriage, regardless of age. An attempt to delete it failed when the recommendation did not obtain the two-thirds needed for amendment.
details.energy_note: Adult at eighteen, or on marriage, whichever comes first.
details.notes: The clause has been in the Constitution since 1979 and its operative scope concerns renunciation of citizenship; the failed deletion vote was not a vote to legalise child marriage. Recorded precisely because the distinction is usually lost.

details.aspect: And the Marriage Act sets no minimum age at all
details.description: The federal Child Rights Act bans child marriage, but the Marriage Act specifies no minimum, and the Child Rights Act must be domesticated state by state - which the highest-prevalence states have not done.
details.energy_note: Three statutes, and the strictest one does not apply where it is needed.

details.aspect: It is the upstream cause of several other issues here
details.description: Early marriage ends schooling (EDU-002), produces the obstructed labour in MAT-002, removes the independent income that would make divorce possible, and sets the household bargaining position for forty years.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings difference.
details.energy_note: One year's decision, forty years of consequence.

details.aspect: Something does work: the community intervention
details.description: A 2026 Nature study reported a big-push community intervention that reduced rates of child marriage by 80%. The problem is not that nothing works.
details.energy_note: Eighty per cent reduction, demonstrated, in a trial.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the four states
details.description: Child marriage prevalence by state: Jigawa 63%, Zamfara 63%, Sokoto 61%, Katsina 61%, against a national figure of 33% before 18 and about 11% before 15. Rural 48% against urban 16%; poorest quintile 67% against richest 6%; 66.7% among women with no formal education against 13% among those completing higher education.
details.energy_note: Eleven times more likely, if you are poor.

issues.title: Inheriting, in theory
issues.category_name: Women's legal status: marriage, inheritance, the bills that failed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: The Supreme Court held in 2014 that customary law barring daughters from inheriting is unconstitutional. Twelve years on, most people affected have not heard of the judgment and compliance is very low.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Ukeje v Ukeje, 2014
details.description: The Supreme Court considered Igbo customary law prohibiting females from inheriting from a father who died intestate, and held the custom unconstitutional as violating section 42. Regardless of the circumstances of a female child's birth, she is entitled to inherit; the contrary custom is void.
details.energy_note: Settled, at the highest court, in 2014.

details.aspect: And the enforcement finding
details.description: A study across five South-Eastern states found most respondents were unaware of the judgment and compliance was very low. Traditional practice still excludes many women from land and property, leaving widows destitute.
details.money_note: Value of the share not received.
details.energy_note: A constitutional right that the village has not heard of.

details.aspect: Litigating against your own family
details.description: Enforcing the right means suing brothers and uncles, in a court in a town, with a lawyer, over years - at the cost of the family relationships that are the only safety net she has.
details.energy_note: Winning the land, and losing everyone.

details.aspect: Which is why most do not
details.description: The rational calculation for a woman with no independent income is to accept the customary outcome rather than spend years and money to obtain a judgment the family will ignore anyway.
details.energy_note: A right that costs more than it is worth to claim.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the land at Nnewi
details.description: Her father died in 2019 without a will. There are four children; she is the only daughter. Her brothers have divided it three ways and are pleasant to her about it. A lawyer in Awka says she would probably win in about four years. She has decided not to, and has not told anyone why.
details.energy_note: Entitled, informed, and choosing the family instead.

issues.title: Being a widow
issues.category_name: Women's legal status: marriage, inheritance, the bills that failed
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Widowhood in much of Nigeria triggers a set of practices that strip property, restrict movement and impose ritual humiliation - enforced by the husband's family and frequently by other women.

details.aspect: What the rites involve
details.description: Being declared unclean and requiring ritual cleansing; confinement for a set period; eating from broken plates; sleeping on the bare floor; shaving the head; wearing prescribed white or dark robes. One account describes 28 days of seclusion without leaving the compound, followed by a further two or five months of mourning depending on local custom.
details.energy_note: Twenty-eight days indoors, and her head shaved.

details.aspect: Levirate, and the property
details.description: Widow inheritance - marrying a late husband's brother or relative, voluntarily or compulsorily - persists in some communities. In-laws, clans and village heads may demand the late husband's property and sell some off ostensibly to fund the burial.
details.energy_note: Widowed on Tuesday, and the property is being valued by Friday.

details.aspect: It is enforced by women as well as men
details.description: The husband's family, kinsmen, and local women's associations all enforce these practices - in some communities the Umuada, the daughters of the lineage. Which removes the assumption that solidarity is automatic.
details.energy_note: The women of the family, enforcing it on the widow.

details.aspect: Compliance is bought with fear of the alternative
details.description: A Delta State study found submission stems from fear of social exclusion, ostracisation, expulsion from the late husband's house or village, and disinheritance of the widow and her children.
details.energy_note: Agreeing to it, because refusing costs the children their home.

details.aspect: Widowers are not subject to any of it
details.description: The asymmetry is total and is the clearest available demonstration that the practices are about property and control rather than mourning.
details.energy_note: He buries her and goes to work on Monday.

details.aspect: The law, and the one case people cite
details.description: VAPP 2015 prescribes up to two years or a N500,000 fine. Cross River's Prohibition of Domestic Violence and Maltreatment of Widows Law No. 6 of 2005 provides a N20,000 fine and 3 years. In Ojukwu v Ojukwu, where relatives tried to evict a widow and her children citing male-only customary inheritance, the court held a widow cannot be treated as a stranger in her own home.
details.energy_note: Illegal, in several statutes, and widely practised.

details.aspect: The scale
details.description: In 2026 the Minister of Women Affairs condemned disinheritance, property grabbing, forced confinement and degrading mourning rites as criminal, noting more than two million widows in Nigeria carry caregiving and breadwinning responsibilities under difficult economic conditions.
details.energy_note: Two million women, and a ministerial statement.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Ojukwu v Ojukwu, and the twenty-eight days
details.description: Where relatives tried to evict a widow and her children citing male-only customary inheritance, the court held that a widow cannot be treated as a stranger in her own home. Alongside the case law, documented practice includes twenty-eight days of seclusion without leaving the compound, followed by a further two or five months of mourning depending on local custom, with the head shaved and prescribed robes worn throughout.
details.energy_note: A judgment in her favour, and twenty-eight days indoors regardless.

details.aspect: The rites end and the position does not
details.description: After the seclusion, the mourning and the cleansing, she returns to a household where the property question was settled during the months she was not permitted to leave the compound. The rites are not only humiliation; they are the interval during which the decisions get made.
details.energy_note: Secluded for the exact period in which it was decided.

issues.title: Cutting
issues.category_name: The body: cutting, widowhood rites and what is done to it
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Female genital mutilation is prohibited by federal law that applies directly in one federal territory, prohibited by state law in thirteen states, and practised in the regions where prevalence is highest.

details.aspect: The legal position
details.description: The VAPP Act came into force on 25 May 2015 and is the first federal law attempting to prohibit FGM nationally - but as a federal law it is directly effective only in the Federal Capital Territory. Thirteen states have their own express prohibitions: Lagos, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti, Bayelsa, Ogun, Delta, Ebonyi, Oyo, Imo, Edo, Cross River and Rivers.
details.energy_note: Banned nationally, in a way that binds one territory.

details.aspect: Where it happens
details.description: Highest prevalence in the South-East and South-West, lowest in the North-East. Types I and II are most common; types III and IV are also carried out, particularly in northern parts.
details.energy_note: Not where most people assume.

details.aspect: The law has not yet reversed it for girls
details.description: Prevalence decreased among women aged 15-49 but rose among girls, from 16.9% in 2013 to 19.2% in 2018, despite the 2015 ban. And because the population is growing, the absolute number of girls cut is increasing even where rates fall.
details.energy_note: The rate fell for women and rose for girls.

details.aspect: The generational signal is real though
details.description: Analysis across MICS rounds from 2007 to 2021 found prevalence declining among both mothers and daughters, with the decrease among daughters relative to mothers suggesting a generational shift possibly influenced by the Act.
details.energy_note: Two datasets, two directions, both recorded.

details.aspect: The obstetric consequence arrives fifteen years later
details.description: Types III and IV in particular complicate delivery, which routes back into MAT-001 and MAT-002 in the next generation.
details.energy_note: Cut at six, in obstructed labour at nineteen.

details.aspect: And it becomes an asylum claim that gets refused
details.description: The Canadian precedent in STA-001 denied a Nigerian woman's FGM-based claim on the basis she could have relocated to a large Nigerian city - so the same practice is both a recognised harm and an insufficient ground.
details.energy_note: Serious enough to be a human rights violation, not serious enough to be refuge.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the thirteen states, and the rising figure for girls
details.description: The VAPP Act came into force on 25 May 2015 but as a federal law binds directly only in the Federal Capital Territory. Thirteen states have their own express prohibitions: Lagos, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti, Bayelsa, Ogun, Delta, Ebonyi, Oyo, Imo, Edo, Cross River and Rivers. Prevalence fell among women aged 15-49 but rose among girls, from 16.9% in 2013 to 19.2% in 2018, despite the ban.
details.energy_note: Banned in 2015, and rising among girls by 2018.

issues.title: Whose body it is treated as
issues.category_name: The body: cutting, widowhood rites and what is done to it
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Across marriage, health and inheritance law the recurring structure is that decisions about a woman's body are made with reference to a man's position.

details.aspect: Consent for treatment
details.description: Spousal consent is commonly requested for surgical and obstetric procedures as a matter of practice rather than law - which means a woman's operation can wait for a man to be located.
details.energy_note: The theatre waiting while somebody phones your husband.

details.aspect: Marital rape is outside the definition
details.description: The VAPP Act expanded the definition of rape significantly but is described in the literature as not covering spousal rape, which leaves the commonest context outside the offence.
details.energy_note: The most likely place for it is the one place it is not the offence.

details.aspect: And the remedy is the family, which is the interested party
details.description: Where the offence is not prosecutable and the police route in POL-003 is closed, the mechanism is family mediation - conducted by the people with the strongest interest in the marriage continuing.
details.energy_note: Judged by the people who want it settled.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the consent form
details.description: She is thirty-eight, has capacity, and is signing for her own hysterectomy. The ward asks, pleasantly, whether her husband is coming, and waits. Nobody says it is required. Nobody proceeds either.
details.energy_note: Nobody said she needed him. Nobody started without him.

issues.title: Menstruation, and what it costs to manage
issues.category_name: The body: cutting, widowhood rites and what is done to it
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Products, privacy, water and disposal are all purchased or absent, and where they are absent the consequence is measured in school days.

details.aspect: The recurring cost against a low income
details.description: Products are bought monthly for roughly forty years, in a household where the purchase competes with food.
details.money_note: Annual spend on menstrual products.
details.energy_note: A monthly purchase that competes with dinner.

details.aspect: School days lost where facilities are absent
details.description: Where a school has no water, no door on the latrine and no disposal, attendance during menstruation becomes impractical - a recurring absence that compounds into the attainment gap in EDU-002.
details.energy_note: A week a month, missed, for want of a door.

details.aspect: Improvised materials cause infection
details.description: Cloth, tissue and rags used repeatedly without adequate washing water produce urinary and reproductive tract infections, which then need the health system in HLT-001.
details.energy_note: An infection produced by the lack of a product.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the week every month
details.description: The school latrine has no door and no water. She works out, at twelve, that missing four days a month is more tolerable than the alternative. By JSS3 she is a term behind in mathematics and is described by her teacher as not strong at it.
details.energy_note: A term behind, and it is recorded as aptitude.

issues.title: Being visible in public as a woman
issues.category_name: The body: cutting, widowhood rites and what is done to it
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Street harassment, transport harassment and the assumption of availability are a continuous tax on moving through public space.

details.aspect: The route, the time and the clothing are all decisions
details.description: Which bus, which hour, which market, what to wear, whether to travel alone. A planning overhead applied to every journey and paid by half the population.
details.energy_note: Three decisions before leaving the house, every time.

details.aspect: Paying for safety where possible
details.description: A taxi instead of a bus, a hired driver, a route with more light. Safety is purchasable, which means it is income-tiered.
details.money_note: Annual premium for safer transport.
details.energy_note: Buying the safer journey, by the trip.

details.aspect: And the restriction is internalised as preference
details.description: After enough years the person describes not going out at night as something she does not enjoy rather than something she has stopped doing. The constraint disappears into the personality.
details.energy_note: A restriction that has learned to call itself a preference.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the last bus
details.description: The 7.40 gets her home in daylight. The 8.20 does not. She leaves work at 7.15 every day regardless of what is unfinished, and has done for six years, and it has been noticed in two appraisals as a lack of commitment.
details.energy_note: Marked down, annually, for catching the earlier bus.

issues.title: Benin City to Italy
issues.category_name: Trafficking, the Gulf, and being sent somewhere and left
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: One city in Edo State became the main hub for sex trafficking between West Africa and Europe. The route is documented, the debt is priced, and the binding mechanism is an oath.

details.aspect: The concentration
details.description: Human rights groups report that 80% of women trafficked to Italy come from Benin City in Edo State, making it the main hub for sex trafficking between West Africa and Europe. UNICRI has cited Italy as the destination for more than 10,000 women trafficked from Benin City.
details.energy_note: Four fifths of them, from one city.

details.aspect: The Mediterranean estimate
details.description: The IOM estimates 80% of Nigerian women travelling to Libya and then attempting the Mediterranean crossing are being trafficked into the European sex trade.
details.energy_note: Four in five of the women on those boats.

details.aspect: The debt, and the oath that enforces it
details.description: Before departure many women take part in a ceremony with a juju priest. Traffickers tell them they must obey or a curse will harm them. The oath-swearing commits the woman to repaying a debt, with violation supposedly leading to death or insanity. Repayment pacts have often been in the range of $40,000-$100,000.
details.money_note: The contracted debt.
details.energy_note: A hundred thousand dollars, secured on a curse.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Oba's revocation, and what followed
details.description: In March 2018 the Oba of Benin, the most powerful traditional ruler in Benin City, issued a curse on traffickers and revoked all juju spells previously administered. The 2024 US Trafficking in Persons report notes traffickers continued performing juju ceremonies as a coercion tactic despite the revocation.
details.energy_note: The oath was cancelled by the man who could cancel it, and they kept using it.

details.aspect: The families are frequently involved
details.description: In many cases parents and close relatives are implicated in the trafficking, which removes the obvious source of rescue and makes reporting an act against your own household.
details.energy_note: Reporting it means reporting your mother.

details.aspect: Refusing to pay has enforcement
details.description: NAPTIP's Benin City office reported cases of intimidation and beatings against women refusing to pay debts, and threats against those asked to testify.
details.energy_note: The debt has collectors, at both ends.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the route shifts rather than closes
details.description: Research indicates the Libya returns increased awareness of the dangers and the difficulty of the crossing dissuaded Edo women from that route - but not from leaving Benin City, as they increasingly travel to other destinations. In one recent case 78 Nigerian girls trafficked to Côte d'Ivoire, some pregnant, were repatriated and received by NAPTIP at Lagos airport.
details.energy_note: Close one route and the destination changes, not the trade.

details.aspect: And the shelter at the end is not a solution
details.description: Human Rights Watch, in 'You Pray for Death', found many rescued victims kept in abhorrent conditions in Nigerian shelters similar to those they faced while trafficked, with authorities failing to provide resources to rebuild. As of March 2024 five organisations met NAPTIP's shelter standards.
details.energy_note: Rescued into conditions resembling the ones she was rescued from.

issues.title: The Gulf contract
issues.category_name: Trafficking, the Gulf, and being sent somewhere and left
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Recruited legally as a housekeeper, flown out with a signed contract, and then unable to leave the country without the employer's permission. The brief calls this being sent somewhere and dumped; the legal name is kafala.

details.aspect: What the system does
details.description: Kafala transfers control of a migrant worker's immigration and employment status to the individual employer. Legally a worker cannot leave the country without the employer's permission, even when experiencing abuse - so reporting to local authorities is rarely an option.
details.energy_note: You may not leave the country without his signature.

details.aspect: The contract terms
details.description: Young Nigerian women are recruited as housekeepers by registered agencies in Nigeria, with contracts reportedly stipulating that for the first 24 months they cannot ask for a salary increase, stop work, run away, or refuse to finish the contract.
details.time_note: The period during which she may not stop.
details.energy_note: Two years in which quitting is a breach of contract.

details.aspect: The conditions, from a survey of fifty
details.description: In one survey of 50 women migrants, all worked seven-day weeks and all had passports confiscated; many reported violence and sexual abuse, and most had paid recruitment fees. Employers cover travel and documentation costs and use that as leverage; agencies profit further by auctioning workers' contracts online.
details.energy_note: Fifty out of fifty, seven days a week, no passport.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - killed by their employers
details.description: In August 2018 two Nigerian migrant domestic staff were killed in Riyadh by their Saudi employers.
details.energy_note: Two women, named in a report, killed by the household they worked in.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the eight who were not allowed to board
details.description: In May 2020, 50 trafficked Nigerian women returned from Lebanon along with 19 nationals stranded by COVID-19 restrictions - but activists reported eight women were blocked from boarding, their employers refusing permission to leave and alleging the women had stolen from them.
details.energy_note: Rescue flight on the runway, and eight of them not allowed on it.

details.aspect: Being abandoned is a distinct outcome from being abused
details.description: Migrants abandoned by their sponsors can be stranded for years because they cannot afford a return flight. Not employed, not deported, not able to leave.
details.money_note: The airfare she cannot raise.
details.energy_note: Left, in a country she cannot leave.

details.aspect: The newer destination, with no embassy
details.description: NAPTIP first flagged exploitative recruitment drives to Iraq in May 2023. There is no Nigerian embassy there, so it coordinates through the consulate in Jordan. Several Nigerian women remain in detention for offences including conflicts with employers and overstaying residence permits.
details.energy_note: Detained in a country where her own government has no office.

details.aspect: The regional trend
details.description: The IOM has documented roughly a 600% increase in potential sex trafficking victims arriving from Africa to the Gulf states in recent decades, with abuse incidents mainly in Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.
details.energy_note: A sixfold increase, and a legal framework that enables it.

issues.title: Knowing, and going anyway
issues.category_name: Trafficking, the Gulf, and being sent somewhere and left
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: Awareness campaigns assume the women do not know. Many do. The decision is made against the alternatives available at home, and the alternatives are the rest of this dataset.

details.aspect: The expectation to provide
details.description: Poverty and lack of opportunity combine with expectations that young women financially support their families, which has driven thousands to seek their fortune abroad. The pressure is familial before it is criminal.
details.energy_note: Sent, by people who love her, to earn.

details.aspect: The returnee who tells the truth is not believed
details.description: A woman who comes back with nothing is read as having failed or having been foolish, not as having been trafficked - so her account does not deter the next departure.
details.energy_note: Warning them, and being heard as making excuses.

details.aspect: Campaigns aimed at awareness miss the actual variable
details.description: Where the choice is between a known risk abroad and a certainty at home, more information about the risk does not change the decision. Changing the alternative would.
details.energy_note: She is not uninformed. She is out of options.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the aunt with the good contact
details.description: Her aunt knows a woman whose daughter is in Oman and sends money every month. The agency in Benin City has an office, a sign and a receipt book. She is nineteen. Everything about it looks like a job, because on paper it is one.
details.energy_note: A registered agency, a signed contract, a receipt.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the WhatsApp voice note from Muscat
details.description: Her friend sends a two-minute voice note that is mostly fine and has eleven seconds in the middle that are not. She listens to it four times. She has already paid the agency NGN 450,000 and her flight is on the 14th.
details.energy_note: Eleven seconds of warning, and a non-refundable deposit.

issues.title: Being suspected of being trafficked
issues.category_name: Trafficking, the Gulf, and being sent somewhere and left
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Nigerian nationality and being female
issues.summary: The mirror of TRF-001: because the route is well documented, young Nigerian women travelling legitimately are screened, doubted and delayed on suspicion of being victims.

details.aspect: The profile is age, sex and nationality
details.description: A young Nigerian woman travelling alone matches a risk profile regardless of her purpose, funding or documents.
details.energy_note: Matching a profile you are not part of.

details.aspect: It produces refusals as well as delays
details.description: A visa officer who suspects trafficking may refuse rather than investigate, because refusal is the lower-risk decision for the officer - and it is recorded as an ordinary refusal.
details.energy_note: Refused for her own protection, on a form that does not say so.

details.aspect: And the good-faith version is still degrading
details.description: Being separated from a queue, questioned about who paid, and asked whether she is being made to travel - by people acting properly - is nevertheless an hour of being treated as possibly owned.
details.energy_note: Correctly screened, and humiliated by it.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the departure desk
details.description: She is twenty-three, travelling alone to a conference in Nairobi with an invitation letter and her own money. The officer asks who is sponsoring her, why she is going alone, and whether her father knows. He is doing his job and she is answering correctly and it takes thirty-five minutes.
details.energy_note: Screened properly, and humiliated by it.

issues.title: A university year that does not happen
issues.category_name: Education, strikes and a certificate nobody abroad trusts
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Public university teaching stops for months at a time. Students are not taught, not examined, not graduated, and not compensated.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - eight months, 2022
details.description: ASUU withdrew its eight-month strike on 14 October 2022, describing the suspension as conditional. Millions of students had been at home since 14 February. The union's president appealed that future strikes 'should not go beyond two days'.
details.energy_note: Two hundred and forty days at home, mid-degree.

details.aspect: The cumulative arithmetic
details.description: Students lost a cumulative four years to 16 ASUU strikes across 23 years, and undergraduates lost at least 13 months of academic calendar under one administration alone.
details.energy_note: Four years of a degree, spent waiting for it to resume.

details.aspect: The cost is borne by the student, not the parties
details.description: Rent continues, living costs continue, and the graduation date moves. Nobody involved in the dispute pays that.
details.money_note: Additional living costs across a strike period.
details.energy_note: Paying rent for a year that is not happening.

details.aspect: For women the delay has a different consequence
details.description: A degree that finishes at 26 instead of 22 collides with marriage pressure, and the commonest resolution is that the degree is abandoned rather than deferred.
details.energy_note: Four extra years, and the pressure does not wait.

details.aspect: And it feeds the credential problem
details.description: Educationists argue the interruptions are why graduates of Nigerian public universities are perceived as half-baked and why Nigerian certificates are not rated highly outside the country - which is EDU-003.
details.energy_note: The strike, and then the discount on the degree it produced.

issues.title: The children who are not in school
issues.category_name: Education, strikes and a certificate nobody abroad trusts
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by anyone living in Nigeria, any gender
issues.summary: Nigeria holds one of the largest out-of-school populations in the world, and the majority of those children are girls.

details.aspect: The scale, with the spread between sources stated
details.description: UNICEF states one in every five of the world's out-of-school children is in Nigeria. Figures range from about 10.5 million aged 5-14 to estimates of 18.3 million, depending on year and age range.
details.energy_note: One in five of all the out-of-school children on earth.

details.aspect: Most of them are girls
details.description: A UNICEF official put it at 60% of 18.5 million being girls, with roughly a 20% difference between male and female enrolment and retention. In the north-east and north-west, female primary net attendance is 47.7% and 47.3% - meaning more than half the girls are not attending.
details.energy_note: More than half the girls in the north, not in school.

details.aspect: The Almajiri system
details.description: Millions of boys are sent far from home to study under traditional Qur'anic teachers and often forced to beg for survival. The system has existed for over 800 years. In 2010 the Universal Basic Education Commission estimated 9.5 million Almajiri nationwide.
details.energy_note: Nine and a half million children, studying and begging.

details.aspect: State-level survey numbers
details.description: Sokoto recorded 249,523 Almajiri and out-of-school adolescent girls; Katsina 148,252 (86,757 boys, 61,495 girls); Jigawa 110,580 (56,159 boys, 54,421 girls).
details.energy_note: A quarter of a million, in one state.

details.aspect: Insecurity is a direct cause
details.description: Attacks on schools and abduction of students deter parents over safety concerns. In the north-east 2.8 million children need education-in-emergencies support and at least 802 schools remain closed.
details.energy_note: Eight hundred schools shut, and the children counted as truant.

details.aspect: The cost lands thirty years later
details.description: Out-of-school at eight produces the literacy gap at eighteen, the informal employment at twenty-five in WRK-001, and the inability to contest the inheritance in WOM-004 at fifty.
details.money_note: Lifetime earnings effect.
details.energy_note: A decision made about a six-year-old, priced at a lifetime.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the state counts, and the closed schools
details.description: Sokoto recorded 249,523 Almajiri and out-of-school adolescent girls; Katsina 148,252 (86,757 boys, 61,495 girls); Jigawa 110,580 (56,159 boys, 54,421 girls). In the north-east 2.8 million children need education-in-emergencies support and at least 802 schools remain closed.
details.energy_note: A quarter of a million in one state, and eight hundred schools shut.

issues.title: A certificate that is discounted abroad
issues.category_name: Education, strikes and a certificate nobody abroad trusts
